subject: Groups & symmetry
labScope: The arrow diagram displays a finite function. Existence of a general descended map follows from representative independence, proved in the lesson.
title: Maps, fibers and well-defined rules
intuition: Before an operation can be a group law, it must be a function: each input has exactly one output.
definition: f:X\to Y,\quad (g\circ f)(x)=g(f(x)),\quad f^{-1}(B)=\{x\in X:f(x)\in B\}
explanation: A function is injective if equal outputs force equal inputs, surjective if every target has an input, and bijective if both hold. The inverse image $f^{-1}(B)$ is defined for every function; it does not assert that an inverse function exists. An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Its classes partition the set, and a rule on classes is well-defined only if changing representatives leaves the output class unchanged.
theorem: f\text{ bijective}\iff f\text{ has a two-sided inverse function}
proof: If $f$ is bijective, each $y$ has exactly one preimage $x$. Define $h(y)=x$. Then $hf=\operatorname{id}_X$ and $fh=\operatorname{id}_Y$. Conversely, if these identities hold, $f(x)=f(x^{\prime})$ implies $hf(x)=hf(x^{\prime})$ and $x=x^{\prime}$; every $y=f(h(y))$ is attained. Thus $f$ is both injective and surjective.
pitfall: The symbols $f^{-1}(B)$ and $f^{-1}:Y\to X$ express different things: an inverse image versus an inverse function. A quotient is a set of classes, not deletion of their elements.
prompt: Which fiber loses an input and which gains it if f(0) changes from 0 to 1?
objective: Distinguish functions, inverse images and well-defined quotient rules.

worked.title: A rule that fails on parity classes
steps: Integers are equivalent when their difference is even. The two classes are even and odd integers.
The proposed map from parity classes to integers, $[a]\mapsto a$, fails: $[0]=[2]$, yet it would assign outputs zero and two.
The map $[a]\mapsto[a+1]$ back to parity classes is well-defined: changing $a$ by an even number changes $a+1$ by an even number. It swaps the two classes.

practice.question: For $f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$, $f(n)=2n$, find $f^{-1}(\{2,3,4\})$. Is $f$ bijective?
practice.hint: Solve each equation separately; a target may have no preimage.
practice.answer: The inverse image is $\{1,2\}$. The map is injective but not surjective, because odd targets have no preimage. Therefore it has no two-sided inverse function.

conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

subject: Groups & symmetry
labScope: Fibers partition the domain because a function assigns one output. Arbitrary congruence classes descend only when each lies inside a fiber.
title: Fibers & equivalence classes
intuition: Why do equal outputs sort every input into exactly one class?
explanation: Let f:X→Y be a function. Define x~x′ exactly when f(x)=f(x′). Empty fibers belong to targets outside the image; they are not equivalence classes.
proof: Reflexivity follows from f(x)=f(x). Symmetry follows by reversing equality; transitivity follows by chaining equalities. If two fibers overlap at z, both target values equal f(z), so the fibers coincide. Otherwise they are disjoint. Every x belongs to its own fiber. Conversely, membership in the same block of a partition is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. The map [x]↦f(x) is well-defined by the defining relation. Equal outputs mean equal classes, so it is injective. Every element of im f has a preimage, so it is surjective onto im f.
pitfall: On Z, define x~y when |x−y|≤1. It is reflexive and symmetric, but 0~1 and 1~2 while 0 is not related to 2. Overlapping neighborhoods do not form equivalence classes.
prompt: Change f(4) to 0: predict the sizes of the fibers of 0 and 1.
objective: Compute fibers, verify equivalence axioms and recover a partition from a function.

worked.title: Remainder fibers
steps: For f:Z→Z/3Z, the classes are 3Z, 1+3Z and 2+3Z.
Each integer lies in exactly one by division with remainder.
The label 1+3Z names an infinite set; choosing 4 instead gives the same set.

practice.question: For f:R→R, f(x)=x², describe the quotient by equal outputs.
practice.hint: Check the hypotheses and try changing representatives.
practice.answer: Positive targets have two opposite preimages; zero has one; negative targets have empty fibers and produce no class. The quotient corresponds to the image [0,∞), not all of R.

conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

subject: Groups & symmetry
labScope: A finite witness disproves the proposed rule. Absence of a witness certifies only this displayed finite domain; the lesson proves the general criterion.
title: Well-defined quotient rules
intuition: If a class has many names, how can a formula using one name define a function?
explanation: Let ~ partition X and ≈ partition Y. A proposed rule F:X/~→Y/≈, [x]↦[f(x)], must send equivalent inputs to equivalent outputs. Equality of output classes, not equality of chosen outputs, is required.
theorem: F([x])=[f(x)]\text{ is well-defined}\iff (x\sim x^{\prime}\Rightarrow f(x)\approx f(x^{\prime}))
proof: Necessity: if [x]=[x′], a function must give one output, hence [f(x)]=[f(x′)]. Sufficiency: assume x~x′ implies f(x)≈f(x′). Pick any representative of an input class. Another representative gives the same output class by assumption, so the output is unambiguous. This proves well-definedness; injectivity, surjectivity and preservation of operations are separate questions.
pitfall: The proposed map Z/2Z→Z, [n]₂↦n, gives 0 and 2 for the same input class. The integer output has no quotient relation that could identify them.
prompt: With f(x)=x mod 3 and parity input classes, compare representatives 0 and 2.
objective: Prove representative independence or disprove a quotient rule with a concrete witness.

worked.title: A parity swap is well-defined
steps: Define F([n]₂)=[n+1]₂.
If n′=n+2k, then n′+1=(n+1)+2k, so the output parity is unchanged.
The map swaps the even and odd classes and is its own inverse.

practice.question: For positive m,n, when is [a]ₘ↦[a]ₙ well-defined?
practice.hint: Check the hypotheses and try changing representatives.
practice.answer: Necessity: 0 and m are equal modulo m, so n must divide m. Sufficiency: every difference divisible by m is then divisible by n. This is a divisibility proof, not a test of a few representatives.

conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

explanation: A group consists of a set $G$ and an operation $G\times G\to G$. Closure says that applying the operation stays in $G$. Associativity says that parentheses do not change a three-term product; it does not say that factors can be reordered. There is an identity $e$, and each $a$ has a two-sided inverse. Integer addition and composition of triangle symmetries are first examples. Matrix groups are a later application.
intuition: Composition is the basic operation: make one move, then another. The group axioms guarantee that moves combine consistently and can be undone.
pitfall: Closure and associativity are different conditions. Positive integers under addition lack an identity; nonnegative integers have an identity but lack additive inverses for positive elements. Nonzero real numbers under addition are not closed: 1 + (−1) = 0.
prompt: Before choosing subtraction modulo 3, predict which axiom will fail.
proof: If $e$ and $f$ are identities, then $e=ef=f$. If $b$ and $c$ are inverses of $a$, then $b=b(ac)=(ba)c=c$ by associativity and the identity laws.

theorem: \text{The identity and each two-sided inverse in a group are unique.}
title: A group is a calculus of reversible moves
subject: Groups & symmetry
objective: Recognise the group axioms in an operation.

worked.title: Addition and a failed operation
steps: On $\mathbb Z$, addition is closed and associative: $(a+b)+c=a+(b+c)$. The identity is $0$ and the inverse of $a$ is $-a$.
On positive integers addition is still closed and associative, but has no identity in the set. On $\mathbb Z$, subtraction is closed but $(3-2)-1=0$ while $3-(2-1)=2$: associativity fails.
If $e,f$ are identities, then $e=ef=f$. If $b,c$ are two-sided inverses of $a$, then $b=b(ac)=(ba)c=c$.

practice.question: Do nonzero real numbers form a group under multiplication? What changes if zero is included?
practice.hint: Find the identity and solve $ax=1$.
practice.answer: Yes: products stay nonzero, multiplication is associative, the identity is $1$, and $a^{-1}=1/a$. Including zero fails the inverse axiom since $0x$ never equals $1$.

labScope: Exhaustive checks prove the axioms for the displayed finite operation. A family-wide result needs the algebraic proof in the lesson.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

definition: o(g)=\min\{m\ge1:g^m=e\},\qquad o(g)=\infty\ \text{if this set is empty}
explanation: The identity and each inverse are unique. Cancellation is allowed on a fixed side. Inverting a product reverses its order. Conjugation changes the frame in which a move is described and preserves its order. Group order counts elements; element order counts repetitions.
intuition: An inverse reverses a move; the order counts how many repeated applications first return to the identity.
pitfall: Two infinite groups need not have the same cardinality. If $a$ and $b$ commute then $(ab)^m=a^mb^m$. Without that hypothesis the formula is not valid in general.
prompt: In C12 choose 8: will its order be 3, 6 or 12?
proof: If $u$ and $v$ are inverses of $g$, then $u=u(gv)=(ug)v=v$. Multiply an equality on the appropriate side to cancel. Since $(hgh^{-1})^m=hg^mh^{-1}$, exactly the same positive exponents yield the identity.

title: Identity, inverses, cancellation and order
subject: Groups & symmetry
objective: Reverse a product correctly and compute an element order.

worked.title: Undo two moves
steps: To undo $ab$, first undo $a$ on the left: $(b^{-1}a^{-1})(ab)=b^{-1}(a^{-1}a)b=e$. On the other side, $(ab)(b^{-1}a^{-1})=e$.
In $C_{12}=\langle g\rangle$, $(g^8)^k=e$ exactly when $12\mid8k$. The least positive such $k$ is $3$.
In the additive group $\mathbb Z$, no positive multiple of $1$ is zero, so $1$ has infinite order.

practice.question: What is the order of $g^9$ in $C_{12}$?
practice.hint: Solve $12\mid9k$ for the least positive $k$.
practice.answer: The least positive solution is $k=4$, since $\gcd(12,9)=3$ and $12/3=4$.

labScope: Cyclic arithmetic is a concrete illustration. The inverse of an arbitrary noncommutative product still reverses factor order, as proved in the lesson.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

definition: H\le G\iff H\ne\varnothing\ \text{and}\ xy^{-1}\in H\quad(\forall x,y\in H)
explanation: The operation is inherited from the ambient group. Every subgroup contains the ambient identity. Intersections of subgroups are subgroups; unions generally are not. Every subgroup of the additive integers consists of all multiples of one nonnegative integer.
intuition: A subgroup is a collection of moves that remains self-contained when moves are composed or reversed.
pitfall: A subset of the correct size need not be a subgroup. Closure under products alone suffices for a nonempty finite subset, but not an infinite one.
prompt: Choose proposed generators and inspect which subset closes under multiplication.
proof: For the subgroup test, choose $x=y$ to obtain $e$, then $e\cdot y^{-1}$ for inverses and $x\cdot (y^{-1})^{-1}$ for products. For integers, choose the least positive member $m$ of a nonzero subgroup and divide every other member by $m$; minimality forces zero remainder.

theorem: H\le(\mathbb Z,+)\Longrightarrow H=m\mathbb Z\ (m\ge0),\qquad b\mathbb Z\le a\mathbb Z\iff a\mid b
title: Closed worlds inside a group
subject: Groups & symmetry

reading.title: Intersections, products and generated subgroups
paragraphs: Intersections preserve the subgroup test: every factor contains the identity and is closed under products and inverses. Thus $\langle X\rangle$ is both the intersection of all subgroups containing $X$ and the set of finite words in elements of $X$ and their inverses.

The product set $HK$ is a subgroup exactly when $HK=KH$. Normality of either factor is sufficient. If both are normal, their product and intersection are normal. Normality is a hypothesis to check, not a consequence of writing two subgroup letters beside each other.

source.title: Alperin & Bell · Groups and Representations

objective: Apply the subgroup test and understand reversed inclusion.

worked.title: Subgroups of the integers
steps: The set $4\mathbb Z$ is nonempty. If $a=4m$ and $b=4n$, then $a-b=4(m-n)$ lies in the set, so it is a subgroup.
For any nonzero subgroup $H\le\mathbb Z$, choose its least positive element $d$. Divide $h\in H$ as $h=qd+r$ with $0\le r<d$. Since $r\in H$, minimality gives $r=0$. Thus $H=d\mathbb Z$.
The remaining subgroup is $\{0\}$. Since every multiple of $12$ is a multiple of $4$, we have $12\mathbb Z\subset4\mathbb Z$.

practice.question: Is the union $2\mathbb Z\cup3\mathbb Z$ a subgroup?
practice.hint: Use the two elements $2$ and $3$.
practice.answer: No: $2+3=5$ is in neither subgroup. The subgroup generated by their union is all of $\mathbb Z$, since $3-2=1$.

definition: \langle S\rangle=\bigcap_{\substack{H\le G\\S\subseteq H}}H=\{s_1^{\varepsilon_1}\cdots s_k^{\varepsilon_k}:s_i\in S,\ \varepsilon_i=\pm1,\ k\ge0\}
explanation: The empty word is the identity. Adding generators can only enlarge the generated subgroup. A subgroup lattice records inclusion, not geometric position: meet is intersection and join is the subgroup generated by both sets. Integer generation is governed by the greatest common divisor.
intuition: Generators are a small vocabulary of moves. Their finite words describe every move that those generators can reach.
pitfall: Joining two subgroups means generating from their union; the union itself can fail closure.
prompt: For g=4 in C12 predict the reachable set; then test r³=e and srs=r⁻¹ in S₃.
proof: Every integer combination of a and $b$ is divisible by their gcd. Bézout's identity expresses the gcd itself as an integer combination, so the generated subgroup contains all its multiples and nothing else.

title: Generators and the subgroup lattice

labScope: The cyclic graph proves finite reachability for the selected Cₙ. The S₃ table checks three defining relations; a separate normal-form upper bound plus six distinct images proves that particular presentation complete.
objective: Distinguish subgroup generation, joins and integer generation; verify relations separately from presentation completeness.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

worked.title: Euclid, Bézout and a non-subgroup union
steps: Euclid: 18=1·12+6 and 12=2·6, so gcd(12,18)=6. Back-substitute 6=18−12; hence ⟨12,18⟩=6Z.
In C₁₂, ⟨4⟩={0,4,8} and ⟨6⟩={0,6}. Their union omits 4+6=10, while their join ⟨4,6⟩=⟨2⟩={0,2,4,6,8,10}.
The S₃ relations r³=s²=e and srs=r⁻¹ hold in the displayed permutations. Completeness additionally requires reducing every word to six normal forms and showing their images are distinct.

practice.question: Find $\langle8,12\rangle$ in the additive integers.
practice.hint: Back-substitute the Euclidean algorithm.
practice.answer: It is $4\mathbb Z$: $4=12-8$, while every combination of eight and twelve is divisible by four.

definition: a\equiv b\pmod n\iff a-b\in n\mathbb Z,\qquad [a]+[b]=[a+b]
explanation: For $n\ge 1$ there are $n$ residue classes. Representatives are labels for whole classes, not new elements. Addition and multiplication are well-defined because replacing representatives by multiples of $n$ changes their sum and product only by multiples of $n$. The additive group is cyclic.
intuition: Residues forget whole turns around a clock while retaining enough information to add consistently.
pitfall: Equality of classes is not equality of their representatives. Modulo 0 means equality, giving a copy of the integers rather than a finite clock.
prompt: Select a cyclic group and compare addition in its table. On paper, replace $a,b$ by $a+n,b+n$ and verify that their sum and product represent the same classes.
proof: If $a^{\prime}=a+kn$ and $b^{\prime}=b+\ell n$, their sum differs from $a+b$ by $(k+\ell)n$. The class of $0$ is the identity; the class of $-a$ is the inverse of the class of $a$.

title: Congruence folds the integer line into a clock
subject: Groups & symmetry
objective: Check representative independence.

worked.title: Changing representatives modulo five
steps: Congruence modulo $5$ means $5\mid a-b$. Reflexivity uses $a-a=0$, symmetry negates the difference, and transitivity adds two differences.
Replace $a,b$ by $a+5u,b+5v$. Their sum changes by $5(u+v)$ and their product by $5(av+bu+5uv)$. Thus both operations on classes are well-defined.
For example $[2][3]=[6]=[1]$; choosing $7$ and $8$ instead gives $[56]=[1]$ again.

practice.question: Why is division by $[0]$ not a well-defined ring operation?
practice.hint: Could any class multiplied by $[0]$ equal $[1]$?
practice.answer: No: multiplication by $[0]$ gives $[0]$ for every input, so $[0]$ has no inverse in a nonzero ring.

explanation: Use $n\ge 2$ here. A unit is a residue with a multiplicative inverse. Bézout's identity turns a gcd calculation into an inverse calculation. For prime $p$ every nonzero residue is a unit. Composite moduli may have nonzero nonunits, so multiplication on all residues is not a group.
intuition: Some residues undo multiplication and some do not. The invertible residues form their own group.
pitfall: Additive order and multiplicative order are different quantities. The unit group of a composite modulus need not be cyclic.
prompt: For modulus 8, compare the order of each unit with the orders in a cyclic group of size 4.
proof: Bézout gives $au+nv=1$ exactly when $\gcd(a,n)=1$; reducing modulo $n$ exhibits $u$ as an inverse. Conversely any congruence $au\equiv 1$ mod $n$ forces every common divisor of a and $n$ to divide 1.

worked.title: Count units at a prime power
steps: Among the $p^k$ residues modulo $p^k$, exactly $p^{k-1}$ are divisible by $p$. Therefore $\varphi(p^k)=p^k-p^{k-1}$.

For coprime $m,n$, CRT identifies a unit modulo $mn$ with an independent pair of units modulo $m,n$, so $\varphi(mn)=\varphi(m)\varphi(n)$. Modulo eight the units are $1,3,5,7$, all nonidentity units having order two.

practice.question: Why is the unit group modulo eight not cyclic of order four?
practice.hint: Check the square of each unit.
practice.answer: All four units square to one. A cyclic group of order four must have a generator of order four; none exists here.

definition: D_n=\langle r,s\mid r^n=s^2=e,\ srs=r^{-1}\rangle=\{r^is^j:0\le i<n,\ j\in\{0,1\}\}
explanation: The course convention is that $D_n$ has 2n elements. Here $r$ rotates counterclockwise through $2\pi /n$ and $s$ reflects in the horizontal axis, with one vertex initially at (1,0). Composition applies the rightmost operation first. There are $n$ rotations and $n$ reflections.
intuition: Every polygon symmetry is determined by where one vertex goes and which way the next vertex lies.
pitfall: Some books call this same group $D_{2n}$. A reflection cannot be continuously connected to a rotation through orthogonal matrices of the plane.
prompt: Build a word, reverse its order, and compare the labeled vertices and matrix products.
proof: The relation $sr=r^{-1}s$ moves every reflection to the right, reducing any word to the displayed form. A symmetry has $n$ choices for the image of a chosen vertex and two for the adjacent vertex; these 2n forms realize all possibilities.

worked.title: Reduce a word of square motions
steps: The four rotations have different images of a chosen vertex. A reflection reverses orientation while a rotation preserves it, so the four reflected forms are distinct from the rotations and from each other. Thus the eight normal forms are genuinely different.

practice.question: If you apply $s$ first and $r$ second, is the matrix product $sr$ or $rs$?
practice.hint: Matrices act on column vectors from the rightmost factor first.
practice.answer: The product is $rs$: it sends $v$ to $r(s(v))$. Chronological order and written product order run oppositely.

explanation: Follow a label until it returns to find a cycle, then repeat on unused labels. The resulting disjoint cycles are unique up to cyclic relabeling and reordering. Disjoint cycles commute; overlapping cycles usually do not. Inverse cycles run backward.
intuition: A permutation routes labels. Disjoint cycles are independent loops in that routing.
pitfall: The lcm formula applies to a decomposition into disjoint cycles. It need not hold for an arbitrary product of overlapping cycles.
prompt: Trace a label through two permutations in both orders and read the final disjoint cycles.
proof: A power of a disjoint-cycle permutation fixes every point exactly when that power is divisible by every cycle length. The smallest such positive exponent is their least common multiple.

title: Permutations, cycles and composition
subject: Groups & symmetry
objective: Compose permutations from right to left.

worked.title: Two overlapping swaps
steps: Let $\sigma=(12)$ and $\tau=(23)$ in $S_3$. For $\sigma\tau$, follow $1\mapsto1\mapsto2$, $2\mapsto3\mapsto3$, and $3\mapsto2\mapsto1$. Thus $\sigma\tau=(123)$.
Reversing the order gives $\tau\sigma=(132)$, so these two swaps do not commute.
Disjoint cycles move disjoint sets. A power fixes everything exactly when its exponent is a multiple of every cycle length; hence the order is their least common multiple.

practice.question: Find the order and sign of $(123)(45)$.
practice.hint: The cycles are disjoint; a three-cycle uses two transpositions.
practice.answer: The order is $\operatorname{lcm}(3,2)=6$. Its sign is $(+1)(-1)=-1$.

labScope: Change the controls to test this finite example. The calculation illustrates the stated result; the proof establishes its general scope.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

definition: \langle g\rangle=\{g^k:k\in\mathbb Z\},\qquad C_n\cong\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z,\qquad C_\infty\cong\mathbb Z
explanation: All cyclic groups are abelian. A finite group is cyclic exactly when it contains an element whose order is the whole group order. Every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic; for each divisor $d$ of $n$ there is one subgroup of $C_n$ of order $d$.
intuition: Repeating one move produces either a closed loop or an unending chain. These are the only cyclic possibilities.
pitfall: An abelian group need not be cyclic. A cycle in an arbitrary drawing need not mean the group itself is cyclic.
prompt: Compare 4 and 5 in C12: which gives all twelve points?
proof: If no positive power of g is e, distinct integer exponents give distinct powers. Otherwise let n be the least positive return. Division with remainder gives exactly n powers. A subgroup H has exponent set {k∈Z:gᵏ∈H}=dZ for some d≥0; in the finite case n∈dZ so d divides n. Therefore H=⟨gᵈ⟩, has n/d elements, and is the unique subgroup of that order. For any k, the least positive m with (gᵏ)^m=e is the least m with n|km, namely n/gcd(n,k). The quotient/first-isomorphism interpretation is revisited later.

title: Cyclic groups and the arithmetic of powers
subject: Groups & symmetry
labScope: The finite table shows every subgroup for the selected Cₙ and the current first-return relation. The exponent/least-positive-return proof in the lesson establishes the classification for all cyclic groups.
objective: Derive finite/infinite cyclic structure from exponents and least return, then enumerate every C₁₂ subgroup and order.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

worked.title: All subgroups of C₁₂
steps: For $C_{12}=\langle g\rangle$, each subgroup is generated by $g^d$ for a divisor $d$ of twelve. Taking $d=1,2,3,4,6,12$ gives orders $12,6,4,3,2,1$.

If a nontrivial subgroup contains $g^k$, take the least positive exponent $d$ occurring. Division with remainder shows every occurring exponent is a multiple of $d$, and $d\mid12$. This proves completeness of the list without assuming a quotient theorem.

practice.question: Which subgroup has order four?
practice.hint: Its generator exponent must be twelve divided by four.
practice.answer: The unique subgroup is $\langle g^3\rangle=\{1,g^3,g^6,g^9\}$.

explanation: A homomorphism sends identity to identity and inverses to inverses. Its image is a subgroup; its kernel records moves invisible in the target. Composition of homomorphisms remains a homomorphism. Determinant maps $\operatorname{GL}_n(F)$ to the multiplicative group $F^\times$, with kernel $\operatorname{SL}_n(F)$.
intuition: A homomorphism translates one language of moves into another without changing how compositions behave.
pitfall: A determinant map has codomain $F^\times$ under multiplication, not all of $F$ as a multiplicative group. An arbitrary labeling need not preserve products.
prompt: Choose a map and compare translating a product with multiplying the two translated elements.
proof: From $\varphi(e)=\varphi(e)^2$, cancel to obtain $\varphi(e)=e$. Apply $\varphi$ to $gg^{-1}=e$ for inverses. For $k\in\ker\varphi$, the identity $\varphi(gkg^{-1})=\varphi(g)e\varphi(g)^{-1}=e$ establishes normality.

title: Homomorphisms preserve composition
subject: Maps & quotients
objective: Check a map preserves the specified operation.

worked.title: Reduction modulo three
steps: The map $f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$ sends $a$ to $[a]$. It preserves addition because $[a+b]=[a]+[b]$.
Its kernel is $3\mathbb Z$ and its image is the whole target. The fiber above $[1]$ is $1+3\mathbb Z$, which is not a subgroup.
The map $a\mapsto a+1$ on the additive integers is not a homomorphism: it sends the identity $0$ to $1$.

practice.question: Is $f([a])=[2a]$ a homomorphism on the additive group $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$? Find its kernel.
practice.hint: Check addition, then solve $2a\equiv0\pmod6$.
practice.answer: It preserves addition and is well-defined modulo six. Its kernel is $\{[0],[3]\}$ and its image is $\{[0],[2],[4]\}$.

explanation: The labels and geometric realization may change while the algebra remains identical. Isomorphisms preserve element orders, group order, commutativity, cyclicity and subgroup structure. Comparing these invariants can disprove a proposed isomorphism, though matching a few invariants does not establish one.
intuition: Two groups are isomorphic when a bijective relabeling matches every multiplication entry.
pitfall: Groups of equal size need not be isomorphic. Identical-looking Cayley graphs without edge labels do not prove an isomorphism.
prompt: Set the cyclic source and target to the same size and choose multiplier one. Every fiber is a singleton. Then change the multiplier to test when the map ceases to be injective.
proof: A bijective homomorphism satisfies $\varphi (g)^m=e$ exactly when $g^m=e$, so element orders agree. $C_{4}$ has an element of order 4, whereas every nonidentity element of $C_{2}\times C_{2}$ has order 2.

worked.title: An explicit cyclic isomorphism
steps: Send $[k]\in\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$ to $r^k$ in the triangle rotation group. Adding exponents corresponds to multiplying rotations, so it is a homomorphism.
The three residues give distinct rotations and exhaust the group, proving injectivity and surjectivity. Its inverse sends each rotation to its exponent modulo three and also preserves the operation.

practice.question: Why does equal cardinality not prove $C_4\cong C_2\times C_2$?
practice.hint: Compare element orders.
practice.answer: The first group contains an element of order four; every element of the second has order at most two. Isomorphisms preserve orders, so these equal-size groups are not isomorphic.

explanation: The jth column is the image of the jth basis vector. Permutation matrices have one 1 in each row and column. This construction is faithful: different permutations give different matrices. It is the first bridge from a group action to a linear representation.
intuition: Replace each label by a basis vector. Routing labels now becomes a linear transformation.
pitfall: Switching between row-vector and column-vector conventions reverses composition conventions unless handled consistently.
prompt: Select a permutation and watch each basis vector move to the column shown in its matrix.
proof: Apply both sides of the product identity to each basis vector: $P_\sigma P_\tau e_j=e_{\sigma (\tau (j))}$. The columns are an orthonormal basis, so the transpose is the inverse, and taking determinants gives determinant squared equal to 1.

title: A permutation becomes a matrix
subject: Groups & symmetry
objective: Read matrix columns as images of basis vectors.

worked.title: The matrix of a three-cycle
steps: For $\sigma=(123)$, the columns are $e_2,e_3,e_1$, so $P_\sigma=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
Thus $P_\sigma(a,b,c)^{\mathsf T}=(c,a,b)^{\mathsf T}$. Applying it three times returns every vector.
On each basis vector, $P_\sigma P_\tau e_j=P_\sigma e_{\tau(j)}=e_{\sigma(\tau(j))}=P_{\sigma\tau}e_j$. Equality on a basis proves equality of the maps.

practice.question: What is the trace of the matrix for $(12)$ acting on three points?
practice.hint: The diagonal has a one exactly at a fixed point.
practice.answer: Only point three is fixed, so the trace is one. The other two basis vectors are swapped.

explanation: A k-cycle can be expressed as $k-1$ transpositions, giving sign $(-1)^{k-1}$. The sign of a product is the product of signs, even for overlapping cycles. Thus every transposition decomposition has the same parity. $A_n$ contains the even permutations.
intuition: Parity extracts one bit from a permutation: whether its matrix preserves or reverses orientation.
pitfall: The sign is not ($-1$) raised to the total number of cycles; a cycle contributes $-1$ exactly when its length is even. $A_{1}$ has order 1.
prompt: Change a cycle length and compare its determinant with the predicted parity.
proof: Multiplicativity follows from determinant. Multiplying by a fixed transposition gives a bijection between even and odd permutations, so precisely half are even when $n\ge 2$.

worked.title: Parity differs from element order
steps: A $k$-cycle is a product of $k-1$ transpositions, so its sign is $(-1)^{k-1}$. Multiplicativity can be justified by the determinant of permutation matrices, using the matrix prerequisite.

The permutation $(12)(34)$ has sign $+1$ and order two. Thus an even permutation can have even order. Since $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma\tau)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\operatorname{sgn}(\tau)$, its kernel $A_n$ is normal.

practice.question: Find the sign of a five-cycle.
practice.hint: Count transpositions in a cycle decomposition.
practice.answer: It is $(-1)^4=+1$; a five-cycle is even.

definition: gH=\{gh:h\in H\},\qquad Hg=\{hg:h\in H\},\qquad gH=kH\iff k^{-1}g\in H
explanation: Left cosets partition the group, and each has the same size as $H$. Right cosets form another partition. In a nonabelian group the two partitions need not agree. A coset usually is not itself a subgroup because it may not contain the identity.
intuition: A coset is a translated copy of a subgroup. Distinct copies fit together without overlap.
pitfall: Elements of $G/H$ are whole cosets. At this stage $G/H$ is a set; it is a quotient group only when $H$ is normal.
prompt: For H={e,(12)}, predict whether (123)H equals H(123).
proof: If $gh=kh^{\prime}$ with $h,h^{\prime}\in H$, then $k^{-1}g=h^{\prime}h^{-1}\in H$, so $gH=kH$. Left multiplication by $g$ is a bijection $H\to gH$, with inverse left multiplication by $g^{-1}$.

worked.title: A nonnormal subgroup of S₃
steps: The map $h\mapsto gh$ is a bijection from $H$ to $gH$, with inverse $y\mapsto g^{-1}y$, so all three cosets have size two.
But $(13)H\ne H(13)=\{(13),(132)\}$. This coset set is not a quotient group under representative multiplication.

practice.question: Why does a subgroup of index two have equal left and right cosets?
practice.hint: Both nonidentity cosets are complements of the subgroup.
practice.answer: For $g\notin H$, both $gH$ and $Hg$ equal $G\setminus H$. For $g\in H$, both equal $H$. Thus every index-two subgroup is normal.

explanation: The index counts cosets. In a finite group, subgroup order and every element order divide group order. A group of prime order is necessarily cyclic. Lagrange restricts possible subgroup sizes but does not promise a subgroup for each divisor.
intuition: Counting a finite group by equal-size coset tiles turns subgroup structure into divisibility.
pitfall: The converse fails: $A_{4}$ has order 12 but no subgroup of order 6. A subset whose size divides $|G|$ need not be closed.
prompt: Predict the number of cosets before choosing the order-two subgroup.
proof: Cosets partition $G$ and each has $|H|$ elements, giving the formula. Apply it to the cyclic subgroup generated by $g$. If $|G|$ is prime, any nonidentity element has order $p$ and generates the whole group.

title: Lagrange counts identical tiles

reading.title: Cyclic subgroups and index multiplication
paragraphs: In $C_n=\langle g\rangle$, each divisor $d$ of $n$ gives exactly one subgroup of order $d$, namely $\langle g^{n/d}\rangle$. In the infinite cyclic group, the nonzero subgroups are $\langle g^d\rangle$, each of index $d$; the trivial subgroup has infinite index.

For $K\le H\le G$, choose representatives for the left cosets of $H$ in $G$ and for those of $K$ in $H$. Their products represent the left cosets of $K$ in $G$ uniquely, giving $[G:K]=[G:H][H:K]$. This bijection also handles infinite index; cancelling infinite cardinalities would not justify the result.

objective: Reconstruct the counting proof and distinguish a necessary divisibility condition from an existence theorem.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

worked.title: A divisor need not be a subgroup order
steps: If $A_4$ had a subgroup of order six, that subgroup would have index two, giving a quotient of order two.

Every three-cycle must map trivially to that quotient because its image order divides both three and two. But three-cycles generate $A_4$: its remaining nonidentity elements are double transpositions, for instance $(123)(124)=(13)(24)$. Thus the quotient map would be trivial, a contradiction.

practice.question: What does Lagrange say about the order of an element in a group of order 18?
practice.hint: Apply the theorem to its cyclic subgroup.
practice.answer: Its order must be one of $1,2,3,6,9,18$. This is a list of necessary possibilities, not a guarantee that all occur.

explanation: Euler's theorem applies to units modulo $n$. Fermat's little theorem is its prime-modulus specialization. The coprimality condition matters: for a nonunit, repeated multiplication need not return to 1.
intuition: Two famous congruences become instances of a single fact: an element order divides its finite group order.
pitfall: The congruence $a^{p-1}\equiv1$ is not valid for a divisible by $p$. The version $a^p\equiv a$ mod $p$ includes that case.
prompt: Choose a unit and track its powers. Compare its actual order with the totient bound.
proof: Apply Lagrange to the element [a] of the finite unit group. For prime $p$ there are exactly $p-1$ nonzero residues and every one is a unit.

theorem: a^{\varphi(n)}\equiv1\pmod n;\qquad a^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p\quad(p\text{ prime},\ p\nmid a)
title: Euler and Fermat from a finite group
subject: Groups & symmetry
labScope: Change the controls to test this finite example. The calculation illustrates the stated result; the proof establishes its general scope.
objective: Explain why Euler’s exponent cannot be applied to an arbitrary residue.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

worked.title: Use coprimality before reducing an exponent
steps: Since $\gcd(2,15)=1$ and $\varphi(15)=8$, Euler gives $2^8\equiv1\pmod{15}$. Hence $2^{19}\equiv2^3\equiv8$.
For a prime $p$, every nonzero residue is a unit, so $a^{p-1}\equiv1$ when $p\nmid a$. Multiplying by $a$ gives $a^p\equiv a$; when $p\mid a$, both sides are already zero modulo $p$.

practice.question: Can Euler’s theorem give $3^8\equiv1\pmod{15}$?
practice.hint: Check the gcd before applying the theorem.
practice.answer: No. Three is not a unit modulo fifteen. In fact its positive powers remain divisible by three and therefore cannot be congruent to one modulo fifteen.

subject: Groups & symmetry
labScope: A relationship map illustrates the stated construction. Work the example and practice independently; arrows are not a proof.
title: Prime divisors produce prime-order elements
intuition: A prime dividing the size of a finite group forces a nonidentity solution of a power equation.
explanation: The theorem supplies an element of prime order, not an element of every divisor order. Its proof counts tuples with product the identity and rotates their coordinates. This cyclic action works even when the group is noncommutative.
proof: Let $X=\{(g_1,\ldots,g_p):g_1\cdots g_p=e\}$. The first $p-1$ entries determine the last, so $|X|=|G|^{p-1}$ is divisible by $p$. Cyclic rotation preserves $X$: from $g_1\cdots g_p=e$ we get $g_2\cdots g_pg_1=g_1^{-1}eg_1=e$. Orbits of the cyclic group of prime order have size one or $p$. Fixed tuples have all entries equal, with $g^p=e$. Therefore their number is divisible by $p$. The identity supplies one, so there must be a nonidentity solution. Its order divides the prime $p$, hence is $p$.
pitfall: Lagrange gives a necessary divisibility condition; Cauchy adds existence for prime divisors. It does not assert a subgroup for every composite divisor.
prompt: Inspect a small group table and find an element of the required prime order. The tuple-counting proof is separate from this finite check.
objective: Explain the counting proof and use its existence conclusion.

worked.title: Apply the theorem at order six
steps: Both two and three divide six. Cauchy therefore supplies an element of order two and an element of order three in every group of order six.
The order-three subgroup has index two and is normal. This is an existence argument; divisibility alone would not construct it.
The theorem does not require an element of order six: $S_3$ has none, although six divides its order.

practice.question: Must a group of order 35 have elements of orders five and seven? Must Cauchy produce one of order 35?
practice.hint: Separate prime and composite divisors.
practice.answer: It produces elements of orders five and seven. It makes no assertion for the composite number 35; deciding that case requires an additional group argument.

conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

explanation: The cyclic groups provide one example at each order. At order 4, absence of an element of order 4 forces every nonidentity element to square to the identity, giving the Klein four-group. At order 6, the nonabelian possibility is the symmetry group of a triangle.
intuition: Small orders leave little room for different multiplication structures, but equal cardinality already stops being decisive at order 4.
pitfall: Classification lists isomorphism types, not every possible naming of their elements. Similar diagrams do not collapse different types.
prompt: Compare $C_{4}$ and the Klein four-group by their element-order distributions.
proof: For |G|=6, Cauchy supplies r of order 3 and s of order 2. H=⟨r⟩ has index two, hence is normal; s is outside H, and the six elements rⁱsʲ with 0≤i<3 and 0≤j<2 are distinct. Conjugation by s acts as an automorphism of C₃, so srs⁻¹ is either r or r⁻¹. In the first case r and s commute and rs has order six, yielding C₆. In the second case r³=s²=e and srs=r⁻¹, the triangle-symmetry relations; mapping r to (123) and s to (12) identifies the six normal forms with S₃. These exhaust the possibilities.

theorem: S_3\cong D_3\cong C_3\rtimes C_2,\qquad C_6\not\cong S_3
title: Classifying the first few group orders

conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

worked.title: Classify groups of order six
steps: Cauchy supplies elements $r$ of order three and $s$ of order two. The subgroup $\langle r\rangle$ has index two and is normal. Its intersection with $\langle s\rangle$ is trivial, and their products exhaust all six elements.

Conjugation by $s$ sends $r$ either to $r$ or $r^{-1}$, the only possible generators. The first case gives commuting factors and $C_6$; the second gives the triangle group $S_3$. These two cases exhaust the possible actions.

practice.question: Why must the element of order two lie outside the order-three subgroup?
practice.hint: Use Lagrange inside the subgroup.
practice.answer: Every element order in the subgroup divides three. An element of order two cannot belong to it.

explanation: For every group G, left multiplication λg(x)=gx is a bijection of the underlying set. Associativity gives λg∘λh=λgh with the right factor acting first. Evaluating at e gives λg(e)=g, so the homomorphism is injective. When |G|=n this is an embedding G↪Sₙ, not a statement about the smallest possible n.
intuition: Let each group element act by left multiplication on the entire group. The multiplication table turns into a collection of permutations.
pitfall: The embedding need not use the smallest possible symmetric group. Do not confuse the regular action on $|G|$ elements with a polygon's action on its vertices.
prompt: For g=(123) and h=(12), predict λg(e), λh(e) and whether λgλh=λgh.
proof: Left multiplication by $g^{-1}$ is the inverse of $\lambda _g$. Associativity gives $\lambda _g\lambda _h(x)=g(hx)=(gh)x$. If $\lambda _g$ is the identity permutation, then $g=\lambda _g(e)=e$.

title: Every finite group permutes itself
subject: Groups & symmetry
labScope: The six-row table constructs the embedding and checks selected compositions. Associativity and evaluation at identity prove the theorem for every group, while the finite table alone proves only this example.
objective: Construct left-regular permutations and prove the embedding, without claiming minimal degree.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

worked.title: Embed C₃ as permutations of itself
steps: Label the elements $1,r,r^2$. Left multiplication by $r$ cycles these three labels, giving the permutation $(1\,2\,3)$. Left multiplication by $r^2$ gives its square.
The products match because $\lambda_g\lambda_h(x)=g(hx)=(gh)x$. If $\lambda_g$ fixes everything, evaluating at the identity gives $g=1$, proving faithfulness.

practice.question: Does this show that three is the smallest possible permutation degree for every group of order three?
practice.hint: Cayley gives an embedding, not automatically minimality.
practice.answer: It gives degree three. Minimality needs a separate observation: $S_1$ and $S_2$ have orders one and two and contain no element of order three.

definition: N\trianglelefteq G\iff gNg^{-1}=N\ \forall g\in G\iff gN=Ng\ \forall g\in G
explanation: Normality is invariance of a whole set under conjugation. It does not say that each element stays fixed. Every subgroup of an abelian group is normal. Every subgroup of index 2 is normal because the only other left or right coset is its complement.
intuition: A normal subgroup is unchanged when its moves are described after a change of frame.
pitfall: Setwise equality $gN=Ng$ does not imply $gn=ng$ for every $n$. Normal subgroups need not lie in the center.
prompt: For A3, predict whether conjugating a 3-cycle by a transposition fixes that element or swaps it.
proof: For index two, if $g\in N$, both $gN$ and $Ng$ equal $N$. Otherwise both equal the complement $G\setminus N$. Thus left and right cosets agree. Also $A_n=\ker(\operatorname{sgn})$ is normal because the sign map is a homomorphism and every kernel is normal.

title: Normality means invariance under conjugation
subject: Maps & quotients

reading.title: Normality is what makes quotient multiplication legal
paragraphs: An index-two subgroup is normal because its only other left and right coset is its complement. More generally, $N\trianglelefteq G$ ensures that replacing representatives in $(xN)(yN)=xyN$ does not change the answer.

A homomorphism sends subgroups to subgroups and has a normal kernel. Conversely every normal subgroup is a kernel, via the quotient map. In a symmetric group, conjugation relabels cycles, so conjugacy is equivalent to equal cycle type.

objective: Test normality through conjugation.

worked.title: A normal subgroup and a near miss
steps: In $S_3$, conjugating a three-cycle gives another three-cycle. Hence $A_3=\{e,(123),(132)\}$ is normal.
By contrast, conjugating $(12)$ by $(13)$ gives $(23)$, which is not in $\langle(12)\rangle$. That subgroup is not normal.
For any homomorphism $f$, if $n\in\ker f$ then $f(gng^{-1})=f(g)e f(g)^{-1}=e$, proving that kernels are normal.

practice.question: Is every subgroup of an abelian group normal?
practice.hint: Simplify $ghg^{-1}$.
practice.answer: Yes. Commutativity gives $ghg^{-1}=h$, so conjugation preserves every subgroup.

labScope: Left/right coset equality tests the same condition. The displayed checks are finite; the proof identifies all homomorphism kernels as normal.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

explanation: Replacing a move by another in its coset should not change the resulting coset of a product. Normality is exactly the condition that makes the induced multiplication independent of representatives. Quotients of abelian groups are abelian, and quotients of cyclic groups are cyclic.
intuition: A quotient remembers only which coset a move belongs to. Multiplication survives when that forgetting is consistent.
pitfall: Removing the elements of $N$ from $G$ does not form $G/N$. The identity in the quotient is the entire coset $N$.
prompt: Compare H={e,(12)} with A3: predict which admits a quotient table.
proof: If $g^{\prime}=gn$ and $h^{\prime}=hm$ with $n,m\in N$, then $g^{\prime}h^{\prime}=gh(h^{-1}nh)m\in ghN$ because $N$ is normal. Thus the product is independent of representatives. Associativity, identity and inverses descend from $G$.

title: Quotient groups identify invisible moves
subject: Maps & quotients
objective: Explain why normality makes coset multiplication well-defined.

worked.title: The sign quotient
steps: The two cosets of $A_3$ in $S_3$ consist of even permutations and odd permutations. Multiplying parity classes gives even-even = even, even-odd = odd, and odd-odd = even.
If representatives change to $gn$ and $hm$, with $n,m\in N$, then $(gn)(hm)=gh(h^{-1}nh)m$. Normality puts the final two factors in $N$, so the product coset is unchanged.
The quotient $S_3/A_3$ is therefore $C_2$, although its elements are cosets, not individual permutations.

practice.question: What is $\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$ as an additive quotient?
practice.hint: List the cosets of $4\mathbb Z$.
practice.answer: The four elements are $4\mathbb Z,1+4\mathbb Z,2+4\mathbb Z,3+4\mathbb Z$. Addition uses representatives modulo four; $1+4\mathbb Z$ generates the group.

definition: \mathbb R/\mathbb Z\cong S^1=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\},\qquad t+\mathbb Z\longmapsto e^{2\pi i t}
explanation: Addition of real parameters becomes multiplication on the unit circle. Choosing $t$ in [0,1) is a way to pick one representative per coset; the interval itself is not closed under ordinary addition. This is also the rotation group SO(2), through the usual rotation matrix.
intuition: Wrap the real line around a circle. Points separated by an integer land at exactly the same place.
pitfall: This is an infinite continuous group. A finite polygon samples only finitely many rotations and is not all of SO(2).
prompt: Vary the angle from zero to a full turn and compare the endpoints. On paper, add $2\pi$ to an angle and check that its sine and cosine are unchanged.
proof: The exponential identity gives the homomorphism. Equality of unit complex numbers is equivalent to arguments differing by an integer multiple of $2\pi$, proving that the fibers are exactly cosets of $\mathbb Z$ and that the displayed map is bijective.

explanation: Automorphisms form a group under composition. Conjugations form its normal subgroup of inner automorphisms. An automorphism that is not inner is called outer. For a cyclic group, sending $g$ to $g^k$ is an automorphism precisely when $k$ is coprime to the group order.
intuition: An automorphism reorganizes a group internally while preserving all multiplication. For a cyclic group, it is a choice of a new generator.
pitfall: The set of outer automorphisms is generally not a subgroup. The outer automorphism group is the quotient $\operatorname{Aut}(G)/Inn(G)$.
prompt: On $C_{8}$, test the exponent maps $k=1,3,5,7$ and compose them.
proof: An automorphism is determined by the image of a generator, which must again generate. Composing $g\mapsto g^k$ and $g\mapsto g^\ell$ multiplies $k$ and $\ell$ modulo $n$. The map $g\mapsto c_g$ has kernel $Z(G)$; apply the first isomorphism theorem.

reading.title: Characteristic subgroups and cyclic automorphisms
paragraphs: An automorphism of $C_n$ sends a generator to another generator, so $\operatorname{Aut}(C_n)\cong(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^\times$. For $n>1$ this is cyclic exactly for $n=2,4,p^k,2p^k$ with $p$ an odd prime. In particular $\operatorname{Aut}(C_p)\cong C_{p-1}$.

A characteristic subgroup is preserved by every automorphism. Characteristic-in-characteristic is characteristic; characteristic-in-normal is normal. Commutators are preserved by automorphisms, so $G^{\prime}$ is characteristic, and $G/N$ is abelian exactly when $G^{\prime}\le N$. Normal-in-normal alone is insufficient: an order-two subgroup of the normal Klein four subgroup of $A_4$ need not be normal in $A_4$.

explanation: The center consists of moves commuting with everything. The centralizer of a subgroup fixes it pointwise by conjugation, while the normalizer fixes it setwise. The normalizer is the largest subgroup of $G$ in which $H$ is normal.
intuition: Centralizing fixes every relevant move individually; normalizing preserves a whole subgroup while possibly rearranging its elements.
pitfall: Normalizer and centralizer need not be equal. If $G/Z(G)$ is cyclic, $G$ is abelian: write each element as a power of one lift times a central element.
prompt: Choose generators for $H$ and a conjugating element $b$. Compare $bHb^{-1}$, the centralizer size and the normalizer size. When is $H$ normal?
proof: Conjugation gives a homomorphism from $N_G(H)$ to Aut(H). Its kernel consists exactly of elements commuting with every member of $H$, namely $C_G(H)$. The first isomorphism theorem identifies the quotient with its image.

title: Centers, centralizers and normalizers

worked.title: Normalize without centralizing
steps: In $D_4$, let $H=\langle r\rangle$. Every reflection normalizes $H$ because $srs^{-1}=r^{-1}$ belongs to $H$.
But a reflection does not centralize $r$, since $r\ne r^{-1}$. The conjugation homomorphism $N_G(H)\to\operatorname{Aut}(H)$ has kernel $C_G(H)$, so its quotient embeds in the automorphism group.

practice.question: What is the image of this map for the square rotation subgroup?
practice.hint: Conjugation either preserves or inverts the generator.
practice.answer: The image has two elements: identity and inversion. The centralizer is the four rotations, while the normalizer is all eight square symmetries.

explanation: For finite-order elements the order formula follows by returning both coordinates to identity. Internally, $G$ is the direct product of $H$ and $K$ if $G=HK$, $H\cap K={e}$, and both are normal. Distinct prime-power factors of a cyclic group separate into independent coordinates.
intuition: In a direct product, two coordinates move independently. Their repetitions synchronize according to a least common multiple.
pitfall: The Cartesian set alone does not determine a direct product. $C_{2}\times C_{2}$ is not cyclic even though it has four elements.
prompt: Compare the orbit of (1,1) in $C_{2}\times C_{3}$ with its orbit in $C_{2}\times C_{4}$.
proof: The element (1,1) in additive $C_m\times C_n$ has order lcm(m,n), which equals mn exactly in the coprime case. When both subgroups are normal with trivial intersection, their commutators lie in the intersection, so the coordinates commute and multiplication $H\times K\to G$ is an isomorphism.

title: Independent coordinates and the Chinese remainder pattern

reading.title: Recognising products and changing semidirect coordinates
paragraphs: If $G=HK$ with $H,K$ normal, then their images in $G/(H\cap K)$ commute and meet trivially. Thus this quotient is the product of $H/(H\cap K)$ and $K/(H\cap K)$. Coprime cyclic factors combine by the Chinese remainder theorem.

In a finite direct product of factors of pairwise coprime orders, any subgroup splits into its intersections with the factors: suitable powers isolate each coordinate. This fails without coprimality; the diagonal in $C_2\times C_2$ is a counterexample.

Reparametrising a cyclic acting group, or conjugating its image in $\operatorname{Aut}(N)$, yields an isomorphic semidirect product. Two distinct involutions generate a dihedral group: their product generates a cyclic subgroup inverted by either involution. The coincident-involution case is degenerate.

worked.title: An internal direct product needs three checks
steps: In $C_6=\langle g\rangle$, the subgroups $H=\langle g^3\rangle$ and $K=\langle g^2\rangle$ have orders two and three, commute, and intersect only in the identity.
The six products $hk$ are distinct and exhaust the group. Thus $(h,k)\mapsto hk$ is an isomorphism $H\times K\to C_6$. The order of $(h,k)$ is the least common multiple of the two coordinate orders.

practice.hint: When do both coordinates return to zero?
practice.answer: Its order is $\operatorname{lcm}(2,4)=4$, while the group has eight elements. It is not a generator.

explanation: The action homomorphism $\alpha$ is part of the data. A trivial action gives the direct product. In $D_n$, the reflection coordinate acts on the rotation coordinate by inversion, explaining the sign change in its multiplication formula. Internally one requires a normal subgroup $N$ and a complement $H$.
intuition: A semidirect product still has two coordinates, but the second changes how the first is composed.
pitfall: The complement $H$ need not be normal. The same underlying set $N\times H$ can support nonisomorphic semidirect products for different actions.
prompt: Predict whether a reflection followed by a rotation equals the reverse order under the inversion action.
proof: Every element has a unique expression $nh$. Multiplication gives $(nh)(n^{\prime}h^{\prime})=n(hn^{\prime}h^{-1})hh^{\prime}$. This is the displayed semidirect-product law, and associativity follows from the homomorphism condition $\alpha(hh^{\prime})=\alpha(h)\alpha(h^{\prime})$.

worked.title: The inversion action builds S₃
steps: Write pairs $(a,b)\in\mathbb Z/3\times\mathbb Z/2$ with multiplication $(a,b)(c,d)=(a+(-1)^bc,b+d)$. The second coordinate decides whether to invert the first.
With $r=(1,0)$ and $s=(0,1)$, we get $r^3=s^2=1$ and $srs=r^{-1}$. Thus this is $S_3$. Replacing the action by the trivial one gives the abelian group $C_3\times C_2\cong C_6$.

practice.question: Why is the action homomorphism part of the data?
practice.hint: Compare the two groups obtained from the same pair of factors.
practice.answer: Different actions give different multiplication laws: one choice produces a nonabelian group and the trivial action produces an abelian group. The factors alone do not determine the semidirect product.

explanation: The subgroup generated by all commutators is normal. Quotienting by it makes every pair commute. This abelianization is the universal part of $G$ visible to homomorphisms into abelian groups.
intuition: The word $xyx^{-1}y^{-1}$ measures the failure of $x$ and $y$ to commute.
pitfall: A commutator subgroup contains products of commutators, not merely the displayed individual commutators. Different books may use the inverse commutator convention.
prompt: Compute the commutator of a rotation and reflection in $D_{4}$, then see what survives in the abelian quotient.
proof: Conjugating a commutator gives $g[x,y]g^{-1}=[gxg^{-1},gyg^{-1}]$, so the subgroup generated by commutators is normal. For a normal subgroup $N$, the cosets $xN$ and $yN$ commute exactly when $[x,y]\in N$. Every homomorphism to an abelian group kills all commutators and therefore factors uniquely through $G/[G,G]$.

worked.title: The abelianization of S₃
steps: Using $[a,b]=aba^{-1}b^{-1}$, take $a=(12)$ and $b=(23)$. Since both are involutions, $[a,b]=(ab)^2=(132)$.
The commutator subgroup therefore contains $A_3$. The sign homomorphism kills every commutator, so it is also contained in $A_3$. Hence $S_3^{\mathrm{ab}}=S_3/A_3\cong C_2$.

practice.question: Why does a homomorphism into an abelian group kill every commutator?
practice.hint: Apply the map to all four factors.
practice.answer: The image is $f(a)f(b)f(a)^{-1}f(b)^{-1}=1$ because the target factors commute. It therefore kills the subgroup generated by all commutators.

explanation: Two elements have the same image exactly when their quotient lies in the kernel. More generally, a map factors uniquely through $G/N$ whenever the normal subgroup $N$ is contained in its kernel. The factor map is injective exactly when nothing more than $N$ is collapsed.
intuition: A homomorphism collapses each kernel coset to a single point. After precisely that collapse, it becomes an isomorphism onto its image.
pitfall: The target is the image, not automatically all of the codomain. A non-surjective map does not yield $G/\ker$ $\varphi \cong H$.
prompt: Map $C_{6}$ to $C_{3}$ and inspect the two-element fibers before collapsing them.
proof: Equality of kernel cosets is equivalent to $\varphi (g)=\varphi (h)$, proving both well-definedness and injectivity of the factor map. Its multiplication law follows from $\varphi$, and surjectivity follows from restricting the target to $\operatorname{im}\varphi$.

title: The first isomorphism theorem: fibers become points

objective: Construct the induced isomorphism, including its inverse obligations.

worked.title: Doubling modulo six
steps: For $f:C_6\to C_6$, $f([a])=[2a]$, the kernel is $K=\{[0],[3]\}$ and the image has three elements.
The induced map sends $[a]+K$ to $[2a]$. If two cosets agree, their representatives differ by an element of $K$, so their images agree: it is well-defined.
Equal images imply the representatives differ by an element of $K$, proving injectivity. Every element of the image has a preimage by definition. Hence $C_6/K\cong\{[0],[2],[4]\}$.

practice.question: Why does the first isomorphism theorem identify the quotient with the image, rather than necessarily the entire codomain?
practice.hint: A homomorphism need not be surjective.
practice.answer: The inclusion $2\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow\mathbb Z$ has trivial kernel but image $2\mathbb Z$, not all of the stated codomain. The induced map is onto its image only.

definition: H\le G,\quad N\trianglelefteq G\quad\Longrightarrow\quad H/(H\cap N)\cong HN/N
explanation: Assume $H\le G$ and $N\trianglelefteq G$. Normality makes $HN$ a subgroup and $N$ normal in $HN$. Restrict the quotient map to $H$: its image is $HN/N$ and its kernel is $H\cap N$.
intuition: To see what $H$ contributes beyond $N$, discard the overlap $H\cap N$. This gives the same group as adjoining $H$ to $N$ and then quotienting by $N$.
pitfall: A product of arbitrary subgroups need not be a subgroup. Here normality of $N$ in $G$ ensures both $HN$ and the quotient $HN/N$ exist.
prompt: Follow the diamond of inclusions. Assume $N$ is normal in $G$: the map $H \to  HN/N$ has kernel $H\cap N$. Which two quotient groups must agree?
proof: Normality of $N$ lets us move its elements past elements of $H$, so $HN$ is a subgroup and $N$ is normal in $HN$. The map $h\mapsto hN$ preserves multiplication and is onto, since $(hn)N=hN$. Its kernel consists of elements of $H$ that lie in $N$, namely $H\cap N$. This is normal in $H$ as a kernel, and the first isomorphism theorem gives the claim.

reading.title: The isomorphism pattern and the butterfly
paragraphs: The map $H\to HN/N$ has kernel $H\cap N$. Hence $H/(H\cap N)\cong HN/N$. Quotienting in stages similarly gives $(G/K)/(H/K)\cong G/H$ for $K\le H$ normal in $G$. Subgroups above a kernel correspond exactly to subgroups of the image.

For $K_i\trianglelefteq H_i$, the two butterfly factors $(H_1\cap H_2)K_1/(H_1\cap K_2)K_1$ and $(H_1\cap H_2)K_2/(H_2\cap K_1)K_2$ are isomorphic: both are images of $H_1\cap H_2$ with the same kernel $(H_1\cap K_2)(H_2\cap K_1)$. This is the local comparison behind refinements of group series. Numbering of the isomorphism theorems varies by source; use the actual maps.

worked.title: Compute both sides in C₁₂
steps: Let $G=\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z$, $H=\langle[2]\rangle$ of order six, and $N=\langle[3]\rangle$ of order four. Their sum is all of $G$ and their intersection is $\{[0],[6]\}$.
The map $H\to G/N$ sends $h$ to $h+N$, with kernel $H\cap N$. Both $H/(H\cap N)$ and $G/N$ have three elements, and the displayed map identifies their generators.

practice.question: Which normality hypothesis makes $HN/N$ a quotient group in the stated theorem?
practice.hint: Look at the ambient subgroup containing both factors.
practice.answer: Assuming $N$ is normal in $G$ ensures $HN$ is a subgroup and $N$ is normal in it. Thus the quotient exists and the restricted quotient map is a homomorphism.

definition: N\le M\le G,\quad N,M\trianglelefteq G,\qquad (G/N)/(M/N)\cong G/M
explanation: Both $N$ and $M$ must be normal in $G$. The map from $G/N$ to $G/M$ sends a smaller coset to the larger coset containing it. Its kernel consists of precisely the smaller cosets lying inside $M$.
intuition: Forgetting $N$ and then forgetting the rest of $M$ has the same effect as forgetting $M$ at once.
pitfall: Normality of $N$ in $M$ and $M$ in $G$ alone does not imply normality of $N$ in $G$. Check both required quotient groups exist.
prompt: Follow both routes from $G$ to $G/M$: quotient directly by $M$, or first by $N$ and then by $M/N$. Why does every element reach the same final coset?
proof: If $gN=hN$, then $h^{-1}g\in N\subseteq M$, so $gM=hM$. This proves that the displayed map is well-defined. It preserves multiplication and is onto; its kernel is $M/N$. Thus $M/N$ is normal in $G/N$, and the first isomorphism theorem supplies the asserted isomorphism.

worked.title: Quotient C₁₂ in two stages
steps: Let $N=\langle[6]\rangle$ and $M=\langle[3]\rangle$ in $C_{12}$. Then $G/N$ has six elements and $M/N$ has two.
Quotienting again gives three elements, just like $G/M$. The map sends the coset of $g+N$ modulo $M/N$ to $g+M$; changing either representative changes nothing.

practice.question: Why is normality of $N$ in $M$ alone insufficient?
practice.hint: The first quotient is $G/N$.
practice.answer: To form that quotient group, $N$ must be normal in all of $G$. Normality is not transitive, so this must be checked separately.

definition: N\trianglelefteq G,\quad \{H\le G:N\le H\}\longleftrightarrow\{K\le G/N\},\qquad H\mapsto H/N,\quad K\mapsto\pi^{-1}(K)
explanation: Assume $N$ is a normal subgroup of $G$. The correspondence preserves inclusion and normality. Subgroups that do not contain $N$ have no place in this bijection. For the integers modulo $n$, divisors of $n$ encode the resulting cyclic subgroup lattice.
intuition: The subgroup lattice of a quotient is the part of the original lattice above the subgroup being collapsed.
pitfall: The theorem does not identify every subgroup of $G$ with a subgroup of $G/N$. Only those containing $N$ participate.
prompt: Select a normal subgroup in the lattice. On paper, retain only subgroups containing it and label each by its quotient; the lab does not automatically build the quotient lattice.
proof: The preimage of a subgroup under $\pi$ is a subgroup containing ker $\pi =N$. Conversely $\pi ^{-1}(\pi (H))=H$ whenever $H$ contains $N$. These inverse maps preserve inclusion. Conjugation passes through $\pi$, giving the equivalence of normality.

worked.title: Lift subgroups from C₆
steps: For $G=C_{12}$ and $N=\langle g^6\rangle$, the quotient is $C_6$. Its subgroups of orders $1,2,3,6$ lift to subgroups of $G$ of orders $2,4,6,12$, all containing $N$.
Explicitly, these are $\langle g^6\rangle,\langle g^3\rangle,\langle g^2\rangle,G$. Taking image under the quotient and taking inverse image are inverse operations on this interval.

practice.question: Why is the trivial subgroup of $G$ absent from the lifted interval?
practice.hint: Every inverse image contains the kernel.
practice.answer: It does not contain the nontrivial subgroup $N$, so it cannot be the inverse image of a quotient subgroup.

definition: G\cong\prod_i C_{p_i^{a_i}}\cong C_{d_1}\times\cdots\times C_{d_r},\qquad d_1\mid d_2\mid\cdots\mid d_r
explanation: Here $G$ is finite abelian; the primes in the first product may repeat. These are elementary-divisor and invariant-factor descriptions. With nontrivial factors and standard ordering, the lists are unique. The course writes the invariant factors in the opposite order, an equivalent convention.
intuition: An abelian group splits into independent prime-power clocks. Several clocks for the same prime need not combine into one.
pitfall: The theorem needs both finiteness and commutativity. Having the right total order does not determine the partition of each prime exponent.
prompt: List the three abelian groups of order 8 and compare their maximum element orders.
proof: Proof idea: split $G$ into its $p$-primary subgroups using Bézout. In an abelian $p$-group, a cyclic subgroup of maximal order has a complement; induct on the remaining order. Uniqueness can be recovered from the sizes of the subgroups killed by each power of $p$.

worked.title: Distinguish the abelian groups of order eight
steps: The partitions $3$, $2+1$, and $1+1+1$ of the exponent three give $C_8$, $C_4\times C_2$, and $C_2^3$. This uses the imported classification theorem.

The maximum element orders are eight, four and two, so the groups are pairwise nonisomorphic. To convert elementary divisors to invariant factors, align prime-power factors from largest to largest and multiply entries with different primes.

practice.question: List the abelian groups of order twelve.
practice.hint: Separate the two-primary part from the three-primary part.
practice.answer: The possibilities are $C_4\times C_3\cong C_{12}$ and $C_2\times C_2\times C_3\cong C_2\times C_6$. The classification theorem ensures the list is exhaustive.

definition: Q_8=\langle a,b\mid a^4=e,\ a^2=b^2,\ ba=a^{-1}b\rangle=\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}
explanation: In $Q_8$, we have $i^2=j^2=k^2=ijk=-1$. There is exactly one element of order $2$, namely $-1$. The six elements $\pm i,\pm j,\pm k$ have order $4$. Its three cyclic subgroups of order $4$ meet in $\{1,-1\}$. Every subgroup of $Q_8$ is normal.
intuition: Order 8 has three independent-clock possibilities and two nonabelian structures. Their involutions distinguish the latter immediately.
pitfall: $Q_{8}$ has no element of order 8. Its unique element of order 2 does not force commutativity or cyclicity.
prompt: Compare the multiplication tables and subgroup lattices of $D_{4}$ and $Q_{8}$.
proof: Proof idea for the nonabelian cases: an order-4 cyclic subgroup has index 2. A lift outside it conjugates its generator to its inverse. The lift squares either to $e$, giving $D_{4}$, or to the central involution, giving $Q_{8}$. $D_{4}$ has five involutions while $Q_{8}$ has one, so they are not isomorphic.

explanation: The same group can act on many sets, and even on the same set in different ways. Polygon symmetries act on vertices, edges and diagonals. The group also acts on itself by left multiplication or by conjugation, which are different actions.

title: A group action is a homomorphism into permutations

reading.title: Every orbit is a coset action
paragraphs: An action is a homomorphism $G\to\operatorname{Sym}(X)$. The left regular action is faithful, proving Cayley. Each action splits uniquely into orbits, and $gG_x\mapsto gx$ identifies an orbit with $G/G_x$. Stabilizers along an orbit are conjugate.

An equivariant map can only enlarge a point stabilizer. More explicitly, a map $G/H\to G/K$ taking $H$ to $aK$ exists exactly when $H\le aKa^{-1}$. The two transitive actions are isomorphic exactly when their stabilizers are conjugate.

objective: Verify an action and identify what is being moved.

worked.title: S₃ acts on three points
steps: Let $X=\{1,2,3\}$ and define $g\cdot x=g(x)$. The identity fixes each point, and $(gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$ by function composition.
The orbit of $1$ is all of $X$, while its stabilizer is $\{e,(23)\}$. The action is transitive but not free.
Only the identity fixes all three points, so the action is faithful. A stabilizer fixes one point; the kernel fixes every point.

practice.question: Let $C_4$ act on two points by sending a generator to their swap. Is the action faithful, free or transitive?
practice.hint: The square of the generator acts as the identity.
practice.answer: It is transitive, but has kernel and each point stabilizer equal to $\{e,r^2\}$. Therefore it is neither faithful nor free.

labScope: These are three different actions of one group. Orbit–stabilizer follows from a coset bijection, not merely from seeing equal products of counts.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

explanation: The orbit is a subset of the acted-on set. The stabilizer is a subgroup of $G$. Points in one orbit have conjugate stabilizers. A transitive action has a single orbit and is equivalent as a $G$-set to the action on cosets of one stabilizer.
intuition: A point's orbit records where it can go; its stabilizer records moves that leave it where it is.
pitfall: The bijection is an isomorphism of $G$-sets, not generally of groups: neither the orbit nor the coset set need have a group structure.
prompt: For a transposition under conjugation, predict orbit size and stabilizer order.
proof: Let $H=G_x$. It is a subgroup: $e$ fixes $x$, and if $a,b$ fix $x$, then $ab^{-1}$ fixes $x$. Define $f:G/H\to Gx$ by $f(gH)=gx$. If $gH=hH$, then $h^{-1}g\in H$, hence $gx=hx$; thus $f$ is well-defined. Conversely, $gx=hx$ implies $h^{-1}g\in H$ and $gH=hH$, giving injectivity. Every point of the orbit is $gx$, giving surjectivity. Each coset has $|H|$ elements via $h\mapsto gh$. For finite $G$, its coset partition therefore gives $|G|=|Gx||H|$. No normality is required: $G/H$ here denotes a set of left cosets, not necessarily a quotient group.

title: Orbit–stabilizer: motion versus symmetry
subject: Groups & symmetry

worked.title: Six permutations, three destinations
steps: In the natural $S_3$ action, the stabilizer of $1$ is $H=\{e,(23)\}$. There are three destinations for $1$.
For each destination exactly two permutations send $1$ there: the remaining two points can be assigned in two ways. Thus $6=3\cdot2$.
The coset $gH$ consists precisely of the permutations sending $1$ to $g(1)$. This explains why the same fiber size occurs at every destination.

practice.question: A cube has 24 rotations and six faces. Find the face stabilizer size and explain what is stabilized.
practice.hint: The action on faces is transitive.
practice.answer: Orbit–stabilizer gives $24/6=4$. These rotations preserve the selected face as a set; they need not fix its four vertices individually.

explanation: The stabilizer under conjugation is the centralizer. Central elements form singleton classes. In $S_n$, two permutations are conjugate exactly when their disjoint cycle types agree. This classification foreshadows characters, which are constant on conjugacy classes.
intuition: Conjugation changes labels while preserving the intrinsic type of a move. Its orbits are conjugacy classes.
pitfall: Having the same order is weaker than having the same conjugacy class. Equal cycle type characterizes conjugacy in $S_n$, not automatically in $A_n$.
prompt: Choose the triangle group $D_3\cong S_3$ and conjugation. Its identity, reflections and nonidentity rotations give class sizes $1,3,2$.
proof: The sum takes one representative from every noncentral conjugacy class. Conjugacy classes partition $G$, and orbit–stabilizer gives the size of each. For permutations, conjugation replaces every cycle entry a by g(a), so it preserves cycle type; matching types permits a relabeling back.

title: Conjugacy classes and the class equation
subject: Groups & symmetry

conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

worked.title: The class equation of S₃
steps: The identity has a singleton class. All three transpositions are conjugate, and the two three-cycles are conjugate. Thus $6=1+3+2$.
The centralizer of a transposition has order two, while the centralizer of a three-cycle has order three. Their indices give the class sizes three and two. The center contains only the identity.

practice.question: Why is the conjugacy class of a central element a singleton?
practice.hint: Write $gxg^{-1}$ using commutativity with $x$.
practice.answer: If $x$ commutes with every $g$, then $gxg^{-1}=x$ for all $g$. Conversely, being fixed under every conjugation means commuting with the entire group.

explanation: The intersection is the core of $H$: the largest normal subgroup of $G$ contained in $H$. The action is defined even when $H$ is not normal, because left multiplication still permutes left cosets. For a finite-index subgroup, the image lies in a finite symmetric group.
intuition: A subgroup with few cosets makes the whole group permute a small set. The kernel is what every coset fails to detect.
pitfall: A nonnormal $H$ still gives a coset action, but it does not give the usual quotient group $G/H$.
prompt: Compare the coset action for a reflection subgroup of $D_{4}$ with that for its rotation subgroup.
proof: An element $g$ fixes aH exactly when $a^{-1}ga$ lies in $H$. Intersecting this condition over all a yields the core. The first isomorphism theorem embeds the quotient by the kernel into $S_n$, and Lagrange gives the divisibility.

title: Coset actions and the core
subject: Maps & quotients
labScope: Change the controls to test this finite example. The calculation illustrates the stated result; the proof establishes its general scope.
objective: Compute the action kernel and explain the factorial-index consequence.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

worked.title: A faithful action with a nonnormal stabilizer
steps: Let $H=\langle(12)\rangle\le S_3$. Left multiplication permutes its three left cosets regardless of whether $H$ is normal.
The three conjugates of $H$ are the three transposition subgroups. Their intersection is the identity, so the coset action is faithful. There is still no quotient-group multiplication on $G/H$.

practice.question: What changes if $H=A_3$?
practice.hint: A normal subgroup is equal to all its conjugates.
practice.answer: The action is on two cosets and has kernel $A_3$. In this case the coset set also carries the quotient group structure $S_3/A_3$.

definition: HgK=\{hgk:h\in H,\ k\in K\},\qquad G=\bigsqcup_{HgK\in H\backslash G/K}HgK
explanation: Double cosets partition $G$, but they need not have equal sizes. Their sizes depend on the overlap between $H$ and $gKg^{-1}$. View them through the action of $H$ on the coset set $G/K$.
intuition: A double coset allows changes on the left by $H$ and on the right by $K$. It is a two-sided orbit.
pitfall: Ordinary cosets all have equal size; double cosets generally do not. A double coset need not be a subgroup.
prompt: Use the coset lab to inspect one subgroup at a time. On paper, take $H=K=\langle(12)\rangle\le S_3$ and enumerate $HgK$; double cosets use two subgroup actions, not ordinary cosets.
proof: The $H$-orbit of $gK$ has stabilizer $H\cap gKg^{-1}$, so it contains $[H:H\cap gKg^{-1}]$ left cosets of $K$. For finite groups each contains $|K|$ elements. Therefore $|HgK|=|H||K|/|H\cap gKg^{-1}|$.

explanation: Both $G$ and $X$ are finite. The group need not act faithfully. A fixed configuration may have many moved positions: only the assigned data must agree after the move. Stabilizers account for the unequal sizes of orbits.
intuition: Instead of choosing one representative from every orbit, count how many configurations each symmetry fixes and average.
pitfall: Dividing $|X|$ by $|G|$ works only for a free action. Symmetric configurations often have smaller orbits and invalidate that shortcut.
prompt: Predict the fixed-coloring count for a nonidentity triangle rotation before opening the table.
proof: Count pairs $(g,x)$ with $gx=x$. Counting first by $g$ sums fixed-point counts. Counting by $x$ sums stabilizer sizes. Each orbit contributes $|\operatorname{Orb}(x)||\operatorname{Stab}(x)|=|G|$, giving the formula.
