title: Burnside counts by fixed points
subject: Groups & symmetry
labScope: Double-count (g,c) with g·c=c: each coloring orbit contributes |G| such pairs. This proves the formula; the table checks a finite instance.
objective: Explain why an element fixing no vertices may still fix many colorings.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

worked.title: Binary colorings of a triangle
steps: The identity rotation fixes all eight binary colorings. Each nonidentity rotation has one three-cycle, so it fixes exactly the two constant colorings.
Burnside gives $(8+2+2)/3=4$ rotational orbits. Dividing eight by three would fail because some colorings have nontrivial stabilizers. Colors are allowed to be unused.

practice.question: How can a rotation with no fixed vertex fix a coloring?
practice.hint: A coloring can be constant on a whole cycle.
practice.answer: It can move vertices carrying the same color. A coloring is fixed when every cycle is monochromatic, so vertex fixed points and coloring fixed points are different counts.

explanation: A rotation by $k$ positions has gcd(n,k) cycles on the $n$ bead positions. A coloring fixed by it must be constant along each cycle, with $q$ choices per cycle. For bracelets, average over all 2n elements of $D_n$, including reflections.
intuition: Necklaces identify rotations; bracelets also identify reflections. The chosen equivalence changes the counting problem.
pitfall: These formulas allow repeated colors and unconstrained color counts. Fixing the number of beads of each color requires a different fixed-point calculation.
prompt: Predict which of the two even-polygon reflection types fixes more colorings.
proof: Burnside gives the necklace formula. For odd $n$ each reflection has $(n+1)/2$ cycles. For even $n$, half the reflections have $n/2+1$ cycles and half have $n/2$ cycles. Their fixed-coloring counts give the two bracelet expressions.

title: Necklaces and bracelets
subject: Groups & symmetry
labScope: Count cycles for every rotation and each reflection type, then average all 2n fixed-coloring counts. The table is the finite calculation.
objective: Derive, rather than recall, the fixed-coloring count for each reflection type.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

worked.title: Six beads in two colors
steps: For rotations of six beads, the cycle counts are $6,1,2,3,2,1$. Fixed-coloring counts sum to $64+2+4+8+4+2=84$, giving fourteen necklaces.

Three reflections pass through opposite beads and have four cycles, fixing sixteen colorings each. Three pass through opposite gaps and have three cycles, fixing eight each. Thus bracelets number $(84+3\cdot16+3\cdot8)/12=13$.

practice.question: How many colors must appear in these counts?
practice.hint: Does the experiment require every available color to be used?
practice.answer: There is no requirement to use both colors. The two monochromatic colorings are included. Prescribing an exact color inventory is a different counting problem.

definition: Z_G(a_1,\ldots,a_n)=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\prod_{j=1}^n a_j^{c_j(g)},\quad c_j(g)=\text{number of length-}j\text{ cycles}
explanation: Let $S_r$ permute the $r$ positions of words on $q$ colors. Two words are in the same orbit precisely when they use each color the same number of times. These orbits are multisets, counted by stars and bars. This provides an elementary instance of the cycle-index method. The multivariate cycle index records each cycle length separately. For a color inventory, substitute $a_j=x_1^j+\cdots+x_q^j$; coefficients count orbits with the prescribed numbers of each color. The worked triangle example derives one such substitution. The displayed rising-product identity is a specialization for the full symmetric group, not the definition of the cycle index.
intuition: A permutation's cycle structure determines how many colorings it fixes. Averaging these powers connects group actions to multisets.
pitfall: Fixed points count as cycles of length one. Omitting them gives wrong coloring counts and traces in permutation representations.
prompt: Predict the number of triangle-rotation orbits with exactly two red and one blue bead.
proof: Fixed words are constant on each cycle, giving $q$ choices per cycle. Burnside counts the orbits; stars and bars counts the same multisets. Multiplying by $r$! gives the product formula for every positive integer $q$, hence as a polynomial identity.

title: Cycle counts turn permutations into counting polynomials
subject: Groups & symmetry
labScope: Each cycle must use one color, contributing xʲ or yʲ. Multiplying cycle factors and averaging is Burnside coefficient by coefficient.
objective: Count colorings with a prescribed inventory, explaining the substitution used.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

worked.title: Use a color inventory, not only a color count
steps: For the three rotations of a triangle, $Z=(a_1^3+2a_3)/3$. A length-$j$ cycle contributes $x^j+y^j$ for two colors with weights $x,y$.
Substitute to get $((x+y)^3+2(x^3+y^3))/3=x^3+x^2y+xy^2+y^3$. The coefficient of $x^2y$ is one, counting the rotational orbit with two beads of the first color and one of the second.

practice.question: Why does a length-three cycle contribute $x^3+y^3$, not $(x+y)^3$?
practice.hint: A fixed coloring must be constant on the cycle.
practice.answer: All three positions must receive the same color. Independent choices at each position would count colorings that the cycle does not fix.

explanation: The tetrahedron has 12 rotations acting on 4 vertices. The cube has 24 rotations acting on 8 vertices. The cube's nonidentity rotations have either four vertex cycles (17 rotations) or two vertex cycles (6 rotations), producing the displayed average. For two colors this gives 23 cube-vertex colorings.
intuition: Color the vertices of a solid and identify colorings related by a rigid rotation. Different rotation axes create different cycle patterns.
pitfall: These count colorings modulo rotations, not colorings fixed by every rotation. Adding reflections changes the acting group to order 48 and changes the count.
prompt: Predict whether a face-axis quarter-turn fixes any vertices and how many binary vertex colorings it fixes.
proof: Cube rotations comprise identity; six quarter-turns about face axes with cycle type $4^{2}$; three half-turns about face axes with type $2^{4}$; eight third-turns about vertex axes with type $1^{2}3^{2}$; and six half-turns about edge axes with type $2^{4}$. Burnside gives the formula. Tetrahedral nonidentity rotations all have two vertex cycles.

title: Rotating tetrahedra and cubes
subject: Groups & symmetry
labScope: Each matrix induces an exact permutation on the chosen feature set. The class table yields (q⁸+17q⁴+6q²)/24 for vertices; this finite ledger illustrates Burnside.
objective: Rebuild one coloring polynomial from a class/cycle table.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

worked.title: Rebuild the cube-vertex count
steps: Cube rotations comprise one identity with eight vertex cycles, six face-axis quarter-turns with two cycles, three face-axis half-turns with four cycles, eight vertex-axis third-turns with four cycles, and six edge-axis half-turns with four cycles.
The resulting count for $q$ colors is $(q^8+6q^2+17q^4)/24$. At two colors this is $(256+24+272)/24=23$. This formula is for vertices and rotations, not faces or all symmetries.

practice.question: Why do the vertex-axis third-turns have four cycles?
practice.hint: Count the fixed endpoints of the rotation axis.
practice.answer: Two vertices are fixed and the other six form two three-cycles. Thus there are four cycles in total.

explanation: The largest power of $p$ dividing $|G|$ is the order of a Sylow $p$-subgroup. More strongly, $G$ contains a subgroup of order $p^j$ for every $0\le j\le a$. The case $j=1$ produces an element of order $p$, which is Cauchy's theorem.
intuition: Prime-power divisors are special: unlike arbitrary divisors, they always occur as subgroup orders.
pitfall: Lagrange's converse is false for general divisors; Sylow supplies the prime-power cases. A Sylow $p$-subgroup is maximal among $p$-subgroups, not necessarily among all proper subgroups.
prompt: Choose p=2 or p=3; predict the required Sylow subgroup order and a class whose centralizer has that p-part.
proof: Write $|G|=p^a m$ with $p\nmid m$. Let $G$ act by left multiplication on subsets of size $p^a$. Their number is $\binom{p^a m}{p^a}$, which is congruent to $m$ modulo $p$: in $\mathbb F_p[X]$, repeated use of $(1+X)^p=1+X^p$ gives $(1+X)^{p^a m}=(1+X^{p^a})^m$, and compare the coefficient of $X^{p^a}$. Thus some subset orbit has size not divisible by $p$. Its stabilizer $H$ has order divisible by $p^a$ by orbit–stabilizer. On the other hand, $H$ acts freely on the selected subset: left multiplication fixes an individual group element only for the identity. Its orbits there have size $|H|$, so $|H|$ divides $p^a$. The two divisibilities force $|H|=p^a$, proving existence. This proof uses finite subsets and finite-set counting; it makes no claim for infinite groups.

title: Sylow existence and Cauchy's theorem
subject: Groups & symmetry
labScope: The table checks one finite group. The guided proof supplies both induction branches, including a central subgroup when p divides |Z(G)|.
objective: Explain where finiteness and the maximal power of p are used.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

worked.title: The p-parts of 24
steps: The order $24=2^3\cdot3$ requires Sylow two-subgroups of order eight and Sylow three-subgroups of order three.

In $S_4$, the eight symmetries of a labelled square form a Sylow two-subgroup; a three-cycle generates a Sylow three-subgroup. These exhibited groups realize the existence theorem, rather than merely passing a divisibility test.

practice.question: What is the order of a Sylow five-subgroup in a group of order 600?
practice.hint: Extract the largest power of five dividing the order.
practice.answer: Since $600=2^3\cdot3\cdot5^2$, the required order is 25.

explanation: More generally, every $p$-subgroup is contained in a conjugate of any chosen Sylow $p$-subgroup. Thus a unique Sylow $p$-subgroup is normal, and a normal Sylow $p$-subgroup is unique. Conjugating subgroups is an action whose stabilizer is a normalizer.
intuition: A finite group can have several Sylow $p$-subgroups, but all have the same internal shape because conjugation moves any one to another.
pitfall: Arbitrary subgroups of the same order need not be conjugate. The maximal $p$-power hypothesis is essential.
prompt: For p=2 in S₃, choose distinct Sylow subgroups P and Q; predict the P-orbit sizes on G/Q and identify a fixed coset.
proof: Let $P$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup and let $H$ be any $p$-subgroup. Make $H$ act on $G/P$ by left multiplication. Every orbit size divides $|H|$ by orbit–stabilizer, so is a power of $p$. Since $p$ does not divide $|G/P|$, at least one orbit has size one. Its fixed coset $gP$ satisfies $g^{-1}Hg\le P$. Thus every $p$-subgroup is contained in a conjugate of $P$. If $H$ is Sylow, its order equals that of $P$, so the containment is equality. This proves conjugacy.

title: Sylow subgroups form one conjugacy orbit
subject: Groups & symmetry
labScope: Fixed gQ means g⁻¹Pg≤Q; equal Sylow orders force equality. The listed S₃ cosets illustrate the general proof.
objective: Reconstruct the proof from the action on G/P without memorizing the conclusion.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

worked.title: A fixed coset forces containment
steps: Let a $p$-subgroup $H$ act by left multiplication on $G/P$, where $P$ is Sylow. Every orbit has prime-power size, while $|G/P|$ is not divisible by $p$. Thus at least one orbit is a singleton.
If $gP$ is fixed, then $hgP=gP$ for every $h\in H$, so $g^{-1}Hg\le P$. If $H$ is also Sylow, equal orders make this containment equality, proving conjugacy.

practice.question: Why can a p-group acting on a set of size not divisible by p not have every orbit nontrivial?
practice.hint: Sum the orbit sizes.
practice.answer: Every nontrivial orbit has size divisible by p. If all orbits were nontrivial, their sum would be divisible by p, contradicting the size of the set.

definition: |G|=p^a m,\ p\nmid m\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n_p\mid m,\qquad n_p\equiv1\pmod p
explanation: These are necessary restrictions, not a promise that every allowed number occurs. Combining the restrictions for different primes with element counting can rule out simplicity. For a group of order 30, having six Sylow 5-subgroups and ten Sylow 3-subgroups would demand too many elements.
intuition: Arithmetic narrows the possible numbers of Sylow subgroups. A count of one immediately reveals a normal subgroup.
pitfall: The count of Sylow subgroups is not the count of elements of $p$-power order. For higher-order $p$-subgroups, intersections can contain nonidentity elements.
prompt: For p=2 in S₃, list the counts satisfying n₂∣3 and n₂≡1 mod 2; predict the actual count.
proof: Conjugation is transitive on Sylow p-subgroups, and its stabilizer at P is N_G(P); hence n_p=[G:N_G(P)] divides [G:P]=m because P is contained in N_G(P). For the congruence, P acts by conjugation on the Sylow set and fixes itself. If P also fixes Q, then P normalizes Q and PQ is a subgroup. Its order |P||Q|/|P∩Q| is a p-power, so Sylow maximality forces PQ=P=Q. Thus P is the sole fixed point. Every other P-orbit has size divisible by p, giving n_p≡1 mod p. These are necessary conditions only. In S₃, n₂=1 and 3 both pass arithmetic, yet three transpositions generate three distinct Sylow 2-subgroups.

title: Sylow counts constrain the whole group
subject: Groups & symmetry

reading.title: Sylow subgroups through normal subgroups
paragraphs: If $N\trianglelefteq G$ and $P$ is Sylow in $G$, then $P\cap N$ is Sylow in $N$ and $PN/N$ is Sylow in $G/N$. Compute orders using $|PN|=|P||N|/|P\cap N|$ and compare their prime parts.

For primes $p>q$, a group of order $pq$ has a normal subgroup of order $p$. It is cyclic unless $q$ divides $p-1$; in that case exactly one additional nonabelian isomorphism type arises from a nontrivial action $C_q\to\operatorname{Aut}(C_p)$.

In $A_5$ the conjugacy-class sizes are $1,15,20,12,12$. No union containing the identity gives a proper nontrivial divisor of $60$, so it is simple. Conversely a simple group of order $60$ can be identified with $A_5$ by an appropriate faithful degree-five action.

labScope: Normalizer and unique fixed-Sylow arguments prove the restrictions. Arithmetic provides necessary candidates, not an existence algorithm.
objective: Distinguish an admissible arithmetic count from a realized Sylow configuration.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

worked.title: Arithmetic leaves a genuine choice
steps: For a group of order twelve, $n_3$ divides four and is congruent to one modulo three. Thus $n_3$ can be one or four; arithmetic alone does not decide.
The cyclic group $C_{12}$ realizes one, while $A_4$ realizes four, generated by its eight three-cycles in pairs. Both arithmetic possibilities genuinely occur here.

practice.question: For a group of order 15, what is $n_5$?
practice.hint: It divides three and is one modulo five.
practice.answer: The only possibility is one, so its Sylow five-subgroup is normal.

definition: G\text{ simple}\iff G\ne\{e\}\ \text{and}\ \{e\},G\text{ are its only normal subgroups}
explanation: A composition series is a finite chain in which each subgroup is normal in the preceding one and each successive quotient is simple. The Jordan–$H$ölder theorem says that any two such series have the same simple factors up to isomorphism and reordering. The source mentions this theorem without proving it.
intuition: Normal subgroups allow a group to be broken into quotient pieces. Simple groups are the nontrivial pieces that cannot be broken further in this way.
pitfall: A composition series requires normality in the preceding subgroup, not necessarily in all of $G$. Composition factors do not by themselves determine the original group.
prompt: Use the $S_4$ subgroup lattice as a reference. On paper, check $1\triangleleft V_4\triangleleft A_4\triangleleft S_4$ and refine $V_4$ with a subgroup of order two. The lattice itself does not certify that a series is a composition series.
proof: For the displayed example, each inclusion is normal in the previous group and the factor orders are 2,3,2,2, hence the factors are cyclic and simple. The general Jordan–$H$ölder uniqueness theorem is stated here, not proved by this example.

title: Simple groups and composition factors
subject: Groups & symmetry

reading.title: Composition factors versus chief factors
paragraphs: A composition series has simple successive factors and only requires each term to be normal in the preceding term. A chief series requires all terms to be normal in the whole group and admits no intervening whole-group normal subgroup. Finite groups have both, by repeatedly choosing maximal permissible terms.

Jordan–Hölder says the multiset of composition factors is independent of the series. Refine two series using intersections and products; the butterfly lemma identifies the factors. A minimal normal subgroup of a finite group is a direct product of isomorphic simple groups, so each chief factor has that form.

For $A_4$, the chief series $1<V_4<A_4$ has an elementary abelian factor of order four. A composition series inserts an order-two subgroup of $V_4$ and has factors $C_2,C_2,C_3$. That inserted subgroup is not normal in $A_4$.

explanation: Every noncentral conjugacy class has size divisible by $p$. The identity is central, so the center cannot have size zero and must have at least $p$ elements. A simple finite $p$-group is therefore exactly a cyclic group of prime order.
intuition: A group whose order is a prime power has enough central structure to start an inductive decomposition.
pitfall: A nontrivial center does not imply that the whole $p$-group is abelian. $D_{4}$ and $Q_{8}$ are nonabelian 2-groups.
prompt: Use the class equation for $D_{4}$ or $Q_{8}$ and locate the central involution.
proof: In the class equation, noncentral class sizes are indices of proper centralizers and hence positive powers of $p$. Thus $p$ divides $|Z(G)|$. If $G$ is simple its nontrivial center must be $G$, making it abelian; a finite simple abelian group has prime order.

theorem: G\text{ a finite simple }p\text{-group}\iff G\cong C_p
title: Finite p-groups have a nontrivial center
subject: Groups & symmetry

reading.title: Centers, maximal subgroups and the Frattini argument
paragraphs: The class equation modulo $p$ proves that a nontrivial normal subgroup of a finite $p$-group meets the center nontrivially. Also $G/Z(G)$ cyclic implies $G$ abelian: representatives are powers of one element times central elements.

Every proper subgroup of a finite $p$-group is properly contained in its normalizer. A maximal subgroup is therefore normal and has index $p$. For an abelian $p$-group, splitting off suitable cyclic factors proves the cyclic prime-power decomposition.

If $N\trianglelefteq G$ and $P$ is Sylow in $N$, conjugation by any $g\in G$ produces another Sylow subgroup of $N$. Conjugacy inside $N$ gives $G=N_G(P)N$, the Frattini argument. It links local Sylow information to global normal structure.

reading.title: The two nonabelian groups of odd prime-cube order
paragraphs: For odd $p$, the two nonabelian groups of order $p^3$ are the upper unitriangular $3\times3$ matrices over $\mathbb F_p$, of exponent $p$, and $C_{p^2}\rtimes C_p$, where the acting generator sends $a$ to $a^{1+p}$. The abelian possibilities are $C_{p^3}$, $C_{p^2}\times C_p$ and $C_p^3$.

In class two, commutators are central, so collection formulas reduce powers of products to powers of their factors and a binomial commutator correction. This distinguishes the two exponent cases. At $p=2$ the nonabelian possibilities are instead the dihedral and quaternion groups of order eight.

The Frattini subgroup $\Phi(P)=P^{\prime}P^p$ records nongenerators; a set generates $P$ exactly when its images span $P/\Phi(P)$ over $\mathbb F_p$. This quotient turns a generating-set question into linear algebra.

labScope: Change the controls to test this finite example. The calculation illustrates the stated result; the proof establishes its general scope.
objective: Explain why a finite p-group has nontrivial center but need not be abelian.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

worked.title: The center of Q₈
steps: In $Q_8$, the classes are $\{1\}$, $\{-1\}$, $\{i,-i\}$, $\{j,-j\}$ and $\{k,-k\}$. The class equation is $8=1+1+2+2+2$.
The center is $\{1,-1\}$. It is nontrivial but not the whole group, showing that nontrivial center does not imply commutativity.

practice.question: Why is the center of every nontrivial finite p-group nontrivial?
practice.hint: Reduce the class equation modulo p.
practice.answer: Every noncentral class has size a positive power of p greater than one. Hence the center size is divisible by p; since it contains the identity, it has at least p elements.

definition: |\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb F_p)|=\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(p^n-p^i),\qquad U_n(\mathbb F_p)=\{I+A:A\text{ strictly upper triangular}\}
explanation: The first column can be any nonzero vector; each later column must avoid the span of its predecessors. In the unitriangular subgroup there are $n(n-1)/2$ arbitrary entries above the diagonal. It captures the entire $p$-part of the general linear group order. Every finite $p$-group $G$ embeds into $U_|G|(F_p)$, although this construction can use a much larger dimension than necessary.
intuition: An invertible matrix is an ordered basis. Counting successive independent columns counts the finite general linear group.
pitfall: Matrix entries and determinants are computed in the finite field, not over the reals. A discrete finite-field matrix grid is not a continuous geometric surface.
prompt: Count $\operatorname{GL}_{2}(F_{2})=6$ and its upper-unitriangular subgroup of order 2. Then compare with $S_{3}$.
proof: For column $i+1$, the span of the preceding independent columns has $p^i$ vectors, leaving $p^n-p^i$ choices. Factoring out $p^i$ from each factor gives total $p$-exponent $0+1+$⋯+($n-1$). Unitriangular matrices have exactly that many free field entries and form a subgroup. For the embedding claim, Cayley's theorem gives a faithful permutation-matrix representation over $F_p$; every $p$-subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}_n(F_p)$ lies in a conjugate of its unitriangular Sylow $p$-subgroup.

theorem: |U_n(\mathbb F_p)|=p^{n(n-1)/2},\qquad U_n(\mathbb F_p)\in\operatorname{Syl}_p(\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb F_p))\qquad G\text{ a finite }p\text{-group}\Longrightarrow G\hookrightarrow U_{|G|}(\mathbb F_p)

subject: Groups & symmetry

worked.title: Count independent columns over 𝔽₃
steps: An invertible $2\times2$ matrix over $\mathbb F_3$ has a nonzero first column: eight choices. The second column must avoid the three vectors in its span: six choices.
Thus $|\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb F_3)|=8\cdot6=48$. The upper-unitriangular matrices form a subgroup of order three, its Sylow three-subgroup.

practice.question: Why are there six invertible matrices over $\mathbb F_2$?
practice.hint: Repeat the column count.
practice.answer: There are three choices for the first nonzero column and two for the second outside its span, giving six.

explanation: A ring in this course need not have a multiplicative identity. The modular tables make the axioms finite and visible: every additive row is a permutation, while a multiplicative row can collapse several inputs.
intuition: Addition lets us combine and undo; multiplication tells us how to transform combinations. Distributivity is the rule that makes these two stories compatible.
pitfall: Multiplication is not assumed commutative. A multiplication table alone does not specify a ring.
prompt: Compare addition and multiplication modulo 6. Which operation can collapse two distinct inputs?
proof: Since $a0=a(0+0)=a0+a0$, additive cancellation gives $a0=0$. Apply distributivity to $(a+(-a))b$ to obtain the sign rule.

title: Two operations, one coherent structure
subject: Rings & arithmetic
objective: Use the ring axioms with explicit conventions.

worked.title: Integers and two-by-two matrices
steps: The integers form a commutative unital ring: addition is an abelian group, multiplication is associative, and multiplication distributes over addition.
The ring $M_2(\mathbb R)$ is unital but noncommutative. For matrix units, $E_{12}E_{21}=E_{11}$ but $E_{21}E_{12}=E_{22}$.
We say when commutativity is required; we do not assume every nonzero ring element has a multiplicative inverse.

practice.question: Is $2\mathbb Z$ closed under the two operations? Does it contain the identity of $\mathbb Z$?
practice.hint: Even sums and products stay even.
practice.answer: It is closed and has additive inverses, but does not contain $1$. Thus it is a nonunital subring under conventions allowing these, and is not a unital subring sharing the integer identity.

The inclusion does not preserve the ambient identity $I_2$. This corner subring is not a left ideal: multiplying $E_{11}$ on the left by $E_{21}$ gives $E_{21}$, outside the corner.

practice.question: Does an additive and multiplicatively closed subset automatically contain the ambient identity?
practice.hint: Use the corner example.
practice.answer: No. Its internal identity can differ from the ambient one, or it can have no identity at all. The chosen subring convention must specify the requirement.

definition: R^\times=\{u:\exists v,\ uv=vu=1\},\qquad a\ne0\text{ is a zero divisor}\iff\exists b\ne0,\ ab=0\text{ or }ba=0
explanation: In integers modulo $n$, a residue is a unit exactly when it is coprime to $n$. For $n=6$, multiplication by 5 permutes all six residues; multiplication by 2 identifies three pairs and kills 3.
intuition: Multiplication by a unit rearranges the ring reversibly. Multiplication by a zero divisor destroys information by sending something nonzero to zero.
pitfall: Zero is excluded from the definition of a zero divisor. A nonunit need not be a zero divisor in an infinite ring: 2 in the integers is neither.
prompt: Choose a multiplier modulo 6, then modulo 7. Can you predict which rows are permutations?
proof: Bézout gives $ab+kn=1$ precisely when a is coprime to $n$. Reducing this equation modulo $n$ constructs the inverse. Conversely an inverse modulo $n$ gives such an integer equation.

title: Units and zero divisors
subject: Rings & arithmetic
objective: Separate units, nonunits and zero divisors.

worked.title: Arithmetic modulo twelve
steps: In $\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z$, $5\cdot5\equiv1$, so $[5]$ is a unit. The units are $[1],[5],[7],[11]$, exactly the classes coprime to twelve.
The nonzero class $[3]$ is a zero divisor since $[3][4]=[0]$ with $[4]\ne[0]$. It cannot be a unit: multiplying this equation by an inverse would give $[4]=[0]$.
In $\mathbb Z$, the element $2$ is neither a unit nor a zero divisor. The three categories must not be conflated.

practice.question: Find the inverse of $[2]$ modulo fifteen.
practice.answer: The inverse is $[8]$. Bézout provides the integer relation and reducing it modulo fifteen verifies the inverse.

explanation: If a finite field has characteristic $p$, the copies of its identity form a copy of the prime field. The whole field is a finite-dimensional vector space over that subfield, so its cardinality is a power of $p$.
intuition: Repeatedly adding the identity traces a clock inside any unital ring. In a domain, the first return to zero cannot occur at a composite time.
pitfall: The field $\mathbb F_{p^2}$ and the ring $\mathbb Z/p^2\mathbb Z$ are never isomorphic: their characteristics are $p$ and $p^2$, respectively. Cardinality alone does not determine ring structure.
prompt: Compare addition in the four-element field with integers modulo 4. What is the additive order of the identity?
proof: In a unital ring, the map $\mathbb Z\to R$, $n\mapsto n1_R$, has kernel $d\mathbb Z$, where $d$ is the characteristic (including $d=0$). In a domain, if a positive characteristic factored as $d=ab$ with $1<a,b<d$, then $(a1_R)(b1_R)=0$ with both factors nonzero, a contradiction. Thus positive characteristic is prime. A finite field is a finite-dimensional vector space over its prime subfield $\mathbb F_p$, and a basis of size $k$ gives exactly $p^k$ elements.

worked.title: Four elements, different characteristics
steps: In $\mathbb F_4$, $1+1=0$, so the characteristic is two. Its additive group is $C_2\times C_2$.
In $\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$, adding one to itself four times first gives zero. Its additive group is $C_4$. The two rings have equal cardinality but cannot be isomorphic.

practice.question: Can a field have characteristic six?
practice.hint: Multiply the classes of two and three.
practice.answer: No. They would be nonzero with product zero, contradicting the domain property of a field.

definition: \text{field}\Rightarrow\text{integral domain};\qquad D\text{ domain}\iff D\ne0,\ 1\in D,\ ab=ba,\ ab=0\Rightarrow a=0\text{ or }b=0
explanation: A division ring requires inverses for every nonzero element but may be noncommutative. A field is a commutative division ring. Finiteness closes the gap between cancellation and invertibility.
intuition: A domain permits cancellation by nonzero factors. A field goes further: every nonzero multiplication can be reversed.
pitfall: The zero ring is neither a field nor an integral domain here. Infinite domains need not be fields.
prompt: Watch multiplication by a nonzero residue modulo a prime. Why must the identity appear somewhere in its row?
proof: For nonzero a, the map $x\mapsto ax$ is injective by cancellation. On a finite set it is therefore surjective, so $1=ax$ for some $x$. Commutativity makes $x$ a two-sided inverse.

theorem: D\text{ a finite integral domain}\Longrightarrow D\text{ a field}
title: Domains, division rings and fields
subject: Rings & arithmetic
objective: Distinguish cancellation from existence of inverses.

worked.title: A domain which is not a field
steps: The integers have no nonzero zero divisors: if $ab=0$, then $a=0$ or $b=0$. But $2$ has no integer inverse, so the integers are a domain and not a field.
In a finite domain, multiplication by a nonzero $a$ is injective: $ax=ay$ gives $a(x-y)=0$ and $x=y$.
An injection from a finite set to itself is surjective. Thus some $x$ satisfies $ax=1$, proving that every finite domain is a field.

practice.question: Why does the same argument not prove that the integers form a field?
practice.hint: Identify the step that uses finiteness.
practice.answer: An injective self-map of an infinite set need not be surjective. Doubling on the integers is injective but misses every odd integer, including one.

explanation: An algebraic number satisfies a nonzero integer polynomial. An algebraic integer satisfies a monic integer polynomial. In a quadratic field, multiplication reduces every occurrence of the square of the new root to $D$.

pitfall: A coefficient plane is a coordinate picture over the rationals; it does not make the quadratic field equal to the real plane as a field.
prompt: Change $D$ and multiply two coordinate pairs. How does the rule for the second basis direction change?
proof: Expand the product with the conjugate. The denominator cannot vanish for a nonzero pair of rational coordinates because that would make $D$ a rational square.

title: Adjoining an algebraic number
subject: Fields & polynomials
objective: Relate minimal polynomial, quotient and extension degree.

worked.title: Adjoin √2 to the rationals
steps: The number $\sqrt2$ satisfies $X^2-2=0$. The rational-root argument shows $X^2-2$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$, so it is the minimal polynomial.
Every element of $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$ is uniquely $a+b\sqrt2$. Hence $\{1,\sqrt2\}$ is a basis and the extension degree is two.

Evaluation gives $\mathbb Q[X]/(X^2-2)\cong\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$. For finite extensions $F\subset K\subset L$, products of an $F$-basis of $K$ with a $K$-basis of $L$ form an $F$-basis of $L$, proving the tower law.

practice.question: Can a degree-three extension contain a degree-two intermediate extension?
practice.hint: Apply the tower law.
practice.answer: No. The degree of an intermediate extension divides the total finite degree, and two does not divide three.

explanation: For Gaussian integers the norm is squared Euclidean distance from zero. For positive $D$ it is an indefinite quadratic expression, so it must not be presented as ordinary length. On the quadratic integer ring, both norm and trace are integers.
intuition: Conjugation exchanges the two algebraic choices of a square root. Norm multiplies these two views; trace adds them.

worked.title: Evaluation at zero
steps: The map $f:\mathbb Z[X]\to\mathbb Z$ given by $f(p)=p(0)$ preserves sums, products and the identity.
Its kernel is $(X)$: a polynomial evaluates to zero exactly when its constant coefficient vanishes, so it is divisible by $X$.
Every integer is the image of a constant polynomial, so the map is onto and $\mathbb Z[X]/(X)\cong\mathbb Z$.

practice.question: What is the kernel of evaluation at one?
practice.hint: Use polynomial division by $X-1$.
practice.answer: The kernel is $(X-1)$. The remainder on division by $X-1$ is the constant $p(1)$, so vanishing at one is equivalent to divisibility.

title: Why ideals absorb multiplication

worked.title: Why 2ℤ is an ideal
steps: The set $2\mathbb Z$ is an additive subgroup, and for any $r\in\mathbb Z$, $r(2a)=2(ra)$ remains even. This is absorption by the ambient ring.
The subring $\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb Q$ is not an ideal: $(1/2)\cdot1$ lies outside $\mathbb Z$. Internal multiplication closure is insufficient.
If an ideal contains a unit $u$, then it contains $u^{-1}u=1$, hence every $r=r\cdot1$. A proper ideal cannot contain a unit.

practice.question: Which ideals of a field are possible?
practice.hint: Every nonzero element of a field is a unit.
practice.answer: Only the zero ideal and the whole field. A nonzero ideal contains a unit and therefore contains one and every element.

explanation: For a commutative unital ring, the ideal generated by a finite set consists of linear combinations with ring coefficients. The product of ideals consists of finite sums of products; it always lies inside their intersection.
intuition: An ideal contains all combinations generated by its seeds. In the integers, ideal inclusion runs opposite to divisibility.
pitfall: The set of individual products need not already be an ideal; finite sums belong in the definition. Intersection equals product under coprimality, not in general.
prompt: Use residue multiplication as a related example. On paper compute $(4)+(6)=(2)$, $(4)\cap(6)=(12)$ and $(4)(6)=(24)$ in $\mathbb Z$, and order these ideals by inclusion.
proof: Each product lies in both ideals by absorption. Bézout identifies the sum in the integers, while membership in both principal integer ideals means being a common multiple.

worked.title: Three different ideal operations
steps: In $\mathbb Z$, $(4)+(6)=(2)$ because $2=6-4$ and all such sums are even. The intersection is $(12)$ because simultaneous multiples are exactly multiples of twelve.
The product is $(24)$: finite sums of products of multiples of four and six are precisely multiples of twenty-four. Thus $(24)\subsetneq(12)\subsetneq(2)$.

practice.question: Why does $I\cap J=IJ$ when $I+J=R$ in a commutative unital ring?
practice.hint: Write one as a sum of an element of each ideal.
practice.answer: Choose $a\in I,b\in J$ with $a+b=1$. For $x\in I\cap J$, $x=xa+xb$ lies in $IJ$. The reverse inclusion always holds, so equality follows.

explanation: Quotienting by a polynomial is a rule for reduction. In the quotient by $X$ squared plus 1, the square of the class of $X$ is -1; every class has a representative of degree at most one.
intuition: A quotient merges elements whose difference lies in an ideal. All calculations remain meaningful because changing a representative only changes the result by an element of that ideal.
pitfall: A quotient imposes an equation on classes; it does not assert that $X$ squared equals -1 in the original polynomial ring.
prompt: Select I in ℤ/12ℤ or F₂[X]. Predict the quotient classes and whether a non-ideal additive subgroup could work.
proof: If $a^{\prime}=a+i$ and $b^{\prime}=b+j$ with $i,j\in I$, then $a^{\prime}b^{\prime}-ab=aj+ib+ij\in I$. Addition is checked similarly. For $\mathbb R[X]/(X^2+1)$, monic division gives a unique linear representative; evaluation at the complex number $i$ identifies the quotient with $\mathbb C$.

title: Quotient rings: making an ideal zero
subject: Maps & quotients
objective: Compute in a quotient and justify multiplication.

worked.title: Dual numbers
steps: In $R=\mathbb R[X]/(X^2)$, every class has a unique form $a+b\varepsilon$, with $\varepsilon=[X]$ and $\varepsilon^2=0$.
Multiply $(a+b\varepsilon)(c+d\varepsilon)=ac+(ad+bc)\varepsilon$. For example $(1+2\varepsilon)(1-2\varepsilon)=1$.
The nonzero element $\varepsilon$ is nilpotent, so this quotient is not a domain or field. The ideal relation changes multiplication, not merely the names of representatives.

practice.question: Which dual numbers $a+b\varepsilon$ are invertible?
practice.hint: Solve the product with $c+d\varepsilon$ equal to one.
practice.answer: Exactly those with $a\ne0$. Their inverse is $a^{-1}-ba^{-2}\varepsilon$. If $a=0$, every product has constant term zero.

worked.title: Lift an ideal modulo twelve
steps: Under $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z$, the ideal generated by $[4]$ is $\{[0],[4],[8]\}$. Its full inverse image is $4\mathbb Z$, which contains $12\mathbb Z$.
Quotienting further gives $(\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z)/([4])\cong\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$. The right-hand side is the quotient by the lifted ideal, not by one chosen representative.

definition: M\text{ maximal}\iff M\ne R\text{ and }(M\subseteq J\triangleleft R\Rightarrow J=M\text{ or }J=R)
explanation: Every proper ideal in a nonzero unital ring lies in a maximal ideal. The proof uses Zorn's lemma: a union of a chain of proper ideals stays proper because otherwise one member would already contain 1.
intuition: A maximal ideal leaves no intermediate ideal after quotienting. In a commutative unital ring, that forces every nonzero residue to become invertible.
pitfall: Commutativity is needed for the field characterization. A simple noncommutative quotient need not be a division ring.
prompt: Compare the ideals generated by 2 and 4 in the integers. Which quotient has every nonzero class invertible?
proof: If a is outside $M$, maximality gives $M+(a)=R$, so $1=m+ab$ and $b$ is an inverse to a modulo $M$. Conversely an inverse to each nonzero class forces any larger ideal to contain 1.

worked.title: Turn maximality into an inverse

The reduction map $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb F_3$ sends two to a unit, so it extends uniquely by $a/2^k\mapsto[a][2]^{-k}$. For instance $1/2$ maps to $[2]$. The general property requires images of S to be units, not injectivity of the original map.

explanation: Here $R$ is a domain and the prime ideal is proper. In the integer example, $1/2$ belongs to the localization at 3, while $1/3$ does not. The nonunits are exactly the fractions with numerator divisible by $p$.

Back-substitute: $6=30-24=30-(84-2\cdot30)=3\cdot30-84$. At each step the pair generates the same ideal, and the nonnegative remainders strictly decrease.

explanation: Compute $z/w$ in the complex plane and round its real and imaginary coordinates to integers. The error in each coordinate is at most one half, so its squared length is at most one half.
intuition: Division in the Gaussian lattice works because every complex number lies close to some lattice point. Rounding creates a remainder shorter than the divisor.
pitfall: This norm argument is special to a lattice with the required covering bound. It does not prove that every quadratic integer ring is Euclidean.
prompt: Compute $(7+5i)/(3+2i)=(31+i)/13$ on paper. Round to $2$, then check the remainder $1+i$ has norm two, smaller than thirteen. Use the field view to check products, not as an automatic division algorithm.
proof: Write $z/w=q+\varepsilon$ with each coordinate of $\varepsilon$ bounded by $1/2$. Multiplicativity of norm gives $N(r)=N(w)N(\varepsilon )\le N(w)/2$. This verifies Euclidean division; norm monotonicity follows since a nonzero Gaussian integer has norm at least 1.

worked.title: Divide 7 + 5i by 3 + 2i
steps: The quotient in $\mathbb C$ is $(7+5i)(3-2i)/13=(31+i)/13$. Rounding real and imaginary parts gives the Gaussian integer two.
The remainder is $(7+5i)-2(3+2i)=1+i$, with norm two, strictly less than the divisor norm thirteen. Nearest-point choices at a tie need not be unique; the norm bound is what the algorithm needs.

practice.question: Why does rounding both coordinates guarantee the norm decreases?
practice.hint: Each coordinate error is at most one half.
practice.answer: The squared distance is at most $1/4+1/4=1/2$. Multiplying by the divisor gives a remainder norm at most half the divisor norm, hence strictly smaller.

definition: R\text{ PID}\iff R\text{ a domain and }\forall I\triangleleft R,\ \exists a\in R,\ I=(a)
explanation: The hierarchy proceeds from fields through Euclidean domains, PIDs and UFDs to domains. Each implication carries more structure than the previous statement alone. The integer polynomial ring separates UFD from PID.
intuition: A principal ideal has one generator that accounts for every element by multiplication. Euclidean descent finds such a generator by choosing the smallest nonzero element of an ideal.
pitfall: The reverse implications fail. In particular (2,X) in the integer polynomial ring is not principal.
prompt: Follow the hierarchy and compare the examples integers, Gaussian integers and the integer polynomial ring.
proof: For Euclidean implies PID choose a nonzero a in $I$ of minimum Euclidean value. Divide any $b$ in $I$ by a; the remainder is in $I$ and cannot have smaller positive value, so it is zero. Hence $I=(a)$.

title: Principal ideals and the domain hierarchy
subject: Rings & arithmetic
labScope: Concept map: arrows record the stated relationships. Calculations in the study task are worked on paper; this map is not a symbolic solver.
objective: Prove a given ideal is principal by the minimum-remainder argument.
conventions: Rings may be noncommutative or lack an identity unless this statement says otherwise. A ring map need not preserve 1 unless explicitly required. Domains and fields are nonzero, commutative and unital; modules over a unital ring are unital.

worked.title: The least-remainder argument
steps: Let $I$ be a nonzero ideal in a Euclidean domain. Choose a nonzero $d\in I$ with minimum Euclidean value. For any $a\in I$, divide $a=qd+r$.
Then $r=a-qd\in I$. A nonzero remainder would have smaller value than $d$, contradicting its choice. Thus every $a$ is a multiple of $d$, so $I=(d)$. The zero ideal is separately $(0)$.

practice.question: Does an ideal being principal imply the whole ring is a PID?
practice.hint: A PID condition quantifies over all ideals.
practice.answer: No. One principal ideal is not enough; every ideal must be principal, and the ring must be a domain.

definition: p\text{ prime}:\ p\mid ab\Rightarrow p\mid a\text{ or }p\mid b;\quad p\text{ irreducible}:\ p=ab\Rightarrow a\in R^\times\text{ or }b\in R^\times
explanation: Both definitions require a nonzero nonunit in a domain. Primes are always irreducible. In a PID the converse holds because an ideal lying above an irreducible principal ideal would provide a factorization.
intuition: Irreducible means an element cannot itself be broken into smaller nonunits. Prime means it can detect a factor in every product it divides.
pitfall: Do not use prime and irreducible interchangeably in an arbitrary domain.
prompt: Inspect 3 in the integer ring with sqrt(-5). Why does its inability to factor not make it prime?
proof: Let $R$ be a commutative domain. If the prime element $p=ab$, then $p\mid a$ or $p\mid b$; say $a=pc$. Cancellation gives $1=cb$, so $b$ is a unit and $p$ is irreducible. Conversely, in a PID every ideal above $(p)$ is $(a)$ for some $a$, with $p=ab$. If $p$ is irreducible then either $a$ is a unit and $(a)=R$, or $b$ is a unit and $(a)=(p)$. Thus $(p)$ is maximal and hence prime. This converse need not hold in a general domain.

title: Prime and irreducible are different tests

worked.title: An irreducible which is not prime
steps: In $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, the norm is $N(a+b\sqrt{-5})=a^2+5b^2$. If $3$ factored into two nonunits, their norms would have to be three and three because $N(3)=9$. But $a^2+5b^2=3$ has no integer solution, so three is irreducible.
Yet $3$ divides $(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})=6$, and divides neither factor: their coefficients are not both divisible by three. Thus three is not prime.

practice.question: Which extra hypothesis makes every irreducible prime in the route proved here?
practice.hint: Use the maximality argument for a principal ideal.
practice.answer: Being a PID suffices. A general domain does not, as this quadratic example shows.

explanation: The four displayed factors are irreducible. The norm a squared plus 5b squared has no values 2 or 3; this prevents each displayed factor from splitting into two nonunits. Their norms 4,9,6,6 also prevent the two factorizations from matching by associates.
intuition: Unique factorisation means that every factorization tells the same story after allowing reordering and multiplying factors by units. Some quadratic integer rings admit genuinely different stories.
pitfall: Here 3 is irreducible but not prime. The official Example 4.13 has a wording error on this point; the preceding Example 4.10 proves the correct distinction.
prompt: Compare the two factorization paths of 6 and test whether any factor on one path is an associate of a factor on the other.
proof: The norm is $N(a+b\sqrt{-5})=a^2+5b^2$. There are no elements of norm $2$ or $3$. A nontrivial factorisation of $2$, $3$, or $1\pm\sqrt{-5}$ would require such a norm, so these elements are irreducible. Units have norm $1$, and associates have equal norms. The irreducibles in $6=2\cdot3=(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ cannot be paired as associates.

The result is $X^3+1=(X+1)(X^2-X+1)$ with remainder zero. At each step the highest surviving degree falls.

intuition: A root means the polynomial contains a linear factor. Repeated roots correspond to repeated copies of that factor, consuming more of the polynomial's degree.

worked.title: A zero divisor breaks the degree bound
steps: Over a field, division by $X-a$ has constant remainder $f(a)$. Thus $a$ is a root exactly when $X-a$ divides $f$. Repeatedly extracting distinct linear factors bounds the number of roots by the degree of a nonzero polynomial.
Over $\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$, the nonzero degree-one polynomial $2X$ vanishes at both zero and two. Its leading coefficient is a zero divisor, so the domain root bound does not apply.

practice.answer: It is zero. Therefore a derivative test must retain its characteristic hypotheses; vanishing derivative does not imply a constant polynomial.

definition: \deg f\in\{2,3\},\ F\text{ a field}:\quad f\text{ reducible}\iff\exists a\in F,\ f(a)=0
explanation: For an integer polynomial with leading coefficient $a_n$ and constant term $a_0$, a rational root $r/s$ in lowest terms must satisfy $r$ divides $a_0$ and $s$ divides $a_n$. This produces a finite test when both coefficients are nonzero.
intuition: A factorization of degree two or three must contain a linear factor. At degree four, two quadratic factors can hide from a root search.
pitfall: No roots does not imply irreducible in degree four: ($X^{2}+1)(X^{2}+2$) has no rational roots but factors over the rationals.
prompt: Select a polynomial and coefficient field. Predict its factors, roots and proof status before revealing the certificate.
proof: Clear denominators in $f(r/s)=0$. Isolating the leading term shows $s$ divides $a_n$ $r^n$, hence $s$ divides $a_n$; isolate the constant term similarly. The low-degree criterion follows because a nontrivial factorization must include degree one.

worked.title: An irreducible quadratic over 𝔽₂
steps: The polynomial $f=X^2+X+1$ has $f(0)=1$ and $f(1)=1$ over $\mathbb F_2$, so it has no root.
A reducible quadratic over a field factors into two linear factors and therefore has a root. Thus $f$ is irreducible.
For degree four, no roots only excludes linear factors. For instance $(X^2+1)^2$ over the reals has no real root but is reducible.

practice.question: Is $X^3+X+1$ irreducible over $\mathbb F_2$?
practice.hint: A reducible cubic has a linear factor.
practice.answer: Yes. At zero its value is one; at one its value is also one. With no root it has no linear factor, which suffices for degree three.

worked.title: Separate content from primitive part
steps: The polynomial $6X^2+9X+3$ has content three and primitive part $2X^2+3X+1=(2X+1)(X+1)$.

If a prime divided every coefficient of a product of two primitive integer polynomials, their nonzero reductions modulo that prime would have zero product in the domain $\mathbb F_p[X]$, a contradiction. This proves the primitive-product lemma used when clearing rational denominators.

explanation: For a monic integer polynomial satisfying these conditions, Eisenstein proves irreducibility over the integers and, by Gauss, over the rationals. A change of variable can expose the criterion even when the original coefficients hide it.
intuition: Reducing modulo a prime can force any hypothetical factors to have constant terms divisible by that prime. Their product would then contain one prime factor too many.
pitfall: Eisenstein is sufficient, not necessary. Failure for one prime or one coordinate system proves nothing about reducibility.
prompt: Select a polynomial and coefficient field. Predict its factors, roots and proof status before revealing the certificate.
proof: By Gauss a nontrivial factorization of a monic integer polynomial may be taken monic and integral. Modulo $p$, their product is $X^n$, so both nonconstant factors have zero constant term modulo $p$. This contradicts $p^{2}$ not dividing $c_0$. Translation $X\mapsto X+1$ is a ring automorphism.

worked.title: Translate before applying the test
steps: The polynomial $X^4+1$ does not meet Eisenstein at two directly. Substituting $X+1$ gives $X^4+4X^3+6X^2+4X+2$.

Two divides every nonleading coefficient, four does not divide the constant term, and two does not divide the leading coefficient. Eisenstein proves the translated polynomial irreducible over $\mathbb Q$. Translation has inverse $X\mapsto X-1$, so it preserves reducibility.

practice.question: Does failure of Eisenstein prove reducibility?
practice.hint: Distinguish sufficient and necessary conditions.
practice.answer: No. It is a sufficient test only. A polynomial can be irreducible without meeting the test in its current coordinates.

definition: \mathbb Z[X]\text{ is a UFD},\qquad (2,X)\subseteq\mathbb Z[X]\text{ is not principal}
explanation: Factor the integer content uniquely, then use unique factorisation over the rational polynomial ring and Gauss's lemma for the primitive part. This gives unique factorisation of every nonzero nonunit integer polynomial.
intuition: Unique factorisation of elements does not mean that every ideal has one generator. Polynomial rings reveal that distinction clearly.
pitfall: A UFD theorem concerns factorization of individual elements. Being a PID is a statement about all ideals.
prompt: Place the ideal (2,X) above its separate generators and explain why neither one can generate the whole ideal.
proof: Gauss's lemma lets primitive factors over $\mathbb Q$ be rescaled to primitive factors in $\mathbb Z[X]$. Comparing contents restricts the remaining ambiguity to units. If $(2,X)=(f)$, then $f$ divides $2$, so $f$ is constant; it also divides $X$, so $f=\pm1$. But $(2,X)$ is proper because every member has even constant term. This contradiction proves that $\mathbb Z[X]$ is not a PID.

worked.title: A UFD need not be a PID
steps: In $\mathbb Z[X]$, suppose $(2,X)=(f)$. Then $f$ divides the constant polynomial two, so it has degree zero. It also divides $X$, forcing that constant to be a unit.

This would make $(2,X)$ the whole ring, but every element of the ideal has even constant coefficient and therefore cannot equal one. Thus the ideal is not principal, although Gauss’s theorem makes $\mathbb Z[X]$ a UFD.

practice.question: What distinguishes the two properties?
practice.hint: One concerns factorization of elements; the other all ideals.
practice.answer: Unique factorization controls elements up to units. The PID property asserts that every ideal has one generator. The former does not imply the latter.

definition: I_1\subseteq I_2\subseteq\cdots\Longrightarrow\exists N,\ \forall n\ge N,\ I_n=I_N
explanation: Throughout this chapter, rings are commutative, nonzero and unital unless another convention is stated. The ascending chain condition is equivalent to every ideal being finitely generated, and to every nonempty collection of ideals having a maximal member. Localisation at the denominator sets used in Chapter 3 also preserves the Noetherian property (Exercise 6.19): generate the contracted ideal in $R$, then divide its generators by 1.
intuition: Keep adding genuinely new constraints or generators to an ideal. In a Noetherian ring this process cannot continue along an infinite strictly increasing chain.
pitfall: Noetherian does not mean the ring is finite or that one bound works for every chain. The integers are infinite and Noetherian.
prompt: Increase the number of generators in the infinite-variable example. Every added variable is genuinely new. Contrast this with the finite-generation condition in the theorem.
proof: If every ideal is finitely generated, the union of an ascending chain has finitely many generators, all present at some single stage; the chain stabilizes there. Conversely, an ideal not finitely generated lets us repeatedly choose a new element outside the ideal generated so far.

worked.title: From an infinite chain to an infinitely generated ideal
steps: In $F[X_1,X_2,\ldots]$, the chain $(X_1)\subsetneq(X_1,X_2)\subsetneq\cdots$ never stabilizes. Setting earlier variables to zero proves that the next variable is not in the previous ideal.

The union is an ideal which cannot have finitely many generators: any finite list would lie in one stage and could not produce the next variable. Conversely, in an ACC ring, repeatedly adding an element outside the current finitely generated ideal must stop, proving every ideal finitely generated.

practice.question: Why does finite generation of every ideal force ACC?
practice.hint: Apply it to the union of an ascending chain.
practice.answer: The union is an ideal with finitely many generators. All of them occur in one chain stage, so that stage contains the union and all later stages coincide.

explanation: Quotients by proper ideals preserve the ascending chain condition through ideal correspondence. In particular every proper quotient of a polynomial ring in finitely many variables over a field is Noetherian.
intuition: Adding finitely many polynomial coordinates does not destroy finite generation of ideals. Even a complicated algebraic set can be cut out by finitely many equations.
pitfall: The theorem does not say every ideal is principal. It also does not extend to infinitely many variables without further hypotheses.
prompt: Follow the arrow from a field to a polynomial ring in finitely many variables, then to a quotient. Which finiteness property survives each step?
proof: Proof idea: collect leading coefficients of polynomials in an ideal into a finitely generated coefficient ideal. Choose polynomials realizing those generators and finitely many lower-degree coefficient generators. Subtract suitable multiples to lower degree, proving these finitely many polynomials generate the whole ideal.

explanation: A field has only its zero prime ideal, so its dimension is zero. In a PID that is not a field, every nonzero prime ideal is maximal; the longest chain is the zero ideal followed by a nonzero prime.
intuition: Dimension is measured by how many genuinely different prime layers can nest. The number counts strict inclusions, not the number of ideals drawn.

prompt: On paper compare $(0)\subsetneq(2)$ in $\mathbb Z$ with $(0)\subsetneq(X)\subsetneq(X,Y)$ in a polynomial ring over a field. A displayed chain proves a lower bound; the upper bound requires a separate theorem.
proof: The zero ideal is prime in every domain. A nonfield PID has an irreducible element; its principal ideal is a nonzero maximal prime. Any other nonzero prime is also generated by an irreducible and maximal, so no longer prime chain exists.

explanation: For the integers the radical is zero. For a local ring it is its unique maximal ideal. In integers modulo 12, the maximal ideals are generated by 2 and by 3; their intersection is generated by 6.
intuition: The Jacobson radical consists of elements invisible in every field quotient by a maximal ideal. Adding their multiples to 1 never destroys invertibility.

worked.title: Compute the radical modulo twelve
steps: The maximal ideals of $\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z$ are generated by two and by three. Their intersection is $\{[0],[6]\}$, so this is the Jacobson radical.
For $x=[6]$, every $1-rx$ is either one or seven, both units modulo twelve. For $x=[2]$, choose $r=[2]$: $1-rx=[9]$ is not a unit, so two fails the universal test.

practice.question: Why must the unit criterion hold for every r, not only r = 1?
practice.hint: One successful value cannot exclude a failing value elsewhere.
practice.answer: The definition requires $1-rx$ to be a unit for all $r$. For $x=2$ modulo twelve, $1-x=11$ is a unit but the choice $r=2$ fails.

explanation: Throughout, the ring is commutative and unital. Its nilpotent elements form an ideal contained in every maximal ideal. If the ring is also Artinian, its Jacobson radical is nilpotent and equals the nilradical. In integers modulo 8, the ideal generated by 2 reaches zero after three powers.
intuition: A nilpotent element disappears after repeated multiplication. A radical ideal can collect these invisible directions even when the ring has many nonzero elements.
pitfall: Commutativity matters: in a matrix ring nilpotent matrices need not belong to the Jacobson radical. Even in a commutative ring, a nil ideal and a nilpotent ideal are different; the Artinian hypothesis supplies a uniform exponent for this radical.
prompt: Multiply 2 repeatedly modulo 8 and compare the sequence of elements with the descending ideals (2), (4), (0).
proof: A nilpotent belongs to every prime ideal: if $x^n\in P$, primality repeatedly gives $x\in P$. The reverse inclusion uses existence of a prime disjoint from the powers of a nonnilpotent element, usually proved by a maximality argument. For commutative Artinian rings, radical nilpotence is a further structural theorem imported here. Stabilization of $J^n$ alone does not prove it is zero; applying the finite-generation version of Nakayama would first require an independent finite-generation argument. We do not use Artinian implies Noetherian to justify a proof of that same implication.

worked.title: Nilpotent elements and a uniform exponent
steps: In $\mathbb Z/8\mathbb Z$, the nilradical is $\{0,2,4,6\}=(2)$. Its cube is zero because every product of three even residues is divisible by eight.

In $F[X_1,X_2,\ldots]/(X_1^2,X_2^2,\ldots)$, every element of the ideal generated by all variables is nilpotent, since it involves only finitely many variables. But products of arbitrarily many distinct variables survive, so that ideal is not nilpotent.

practice.question: What extra conclusion does a nilpotent ideal give beyond a nil ideal?
practice.hint: Compare the order of the quantifiers.
practice.answer: A nilpotent ideal has one fixed exponent for all products of ideal elements. In a nil ideal, each element has some vanishing power, which may depend on that element.

definition: I_1\supseteq I_2\supseteq\cdots\Longrightarrow\exists N,\ \forall n\ge N,\ I_n=I_N
explanation: The condition is equivalent to every nonempty collection of ideals having a minimal member. Finite rings are examples, but an Artinian ring need not be a finite set: every field is Artinian.
intuition: The Artinian condition prevents an endless sequence of smaller ideals. It is stronger than the Noetherian condition for the commutative rings studied here.
pitfall: An animation that shows finitely many steps cannot establish stabilization of every infinite chain. The proof must use the algebraic condition.
prompt: Compare powers of (2) in the integers and modulo 16. Why does one chain terminate at zero and the other not?
proof: Every ideal of the integers is principal, so ascending chains stabilize. The displayed descending chain never stabilizes because no power of 2 is an integer multiple of a strictly higher power.

intuition: An Artinian ring has only finitely many maximal locations. The Chinese remainder theorem separates them, while nilpotent directions remain inside each local piece.

explanation: A left $R$-module is an abelian group equipped with this action. The ring acts on itself by left multiplication; its submodules are left ideals. Matrix multiplication makes column vectors a module over the full matrix ring.
intuition: A module turns ring elements into compatible additive transformations. Vector spaces are the special case where the scalars form a field.
pitfall: Units of $R$ always induce invertible additive operators on an $R$-module. A nonunit may also act invertibly on a particular module: $2$ acts as its own inverse on $\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$, although it is not a unit of $\mathbb Z$. On the regular module $R$, invertibility of left multiplication is equivalent to being a unit. We require $1v=v$ for unital modules.

proof: The module laws for matrices are exactly distributivity and associativity of matrix multiplication. For the regular module, closure under the scalar action is precisely closure under multiplication from the left.

worked.title: A nonunit acts invertibly
steps: Take $R=\mathbb Z$ and $M=\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$. The scalar $2$ sends $[0]\mapsto[0]$, $[1]\mapsto[2]$, and $[2]\mapsto[1]$.
Applying this action twice multiplies by four, which equals one modulo three. Thus it is an invertible additive operator.
But $2$ is not a unit of $\mathbb Z$. The action map $R\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Z}(M)$ can send a nonunit to a unit.

practice.question: How does multiplication by three act on the same module?
practice.hint: Reduce $3a$ modulo three.
practice.answer: It is the zero operator, so it is not invertible on this nonzero module. Module axioms allow such scalar actions.

definition: W\le M,\quad rW\subseteq W\ (\forall r\in R),\qquad r(v+W)=rv+W
explanation: For a vector space with a chosen linear operator $T$, we may let $X$ act as $T$ to obtain an $F[X]$-module. Its submodules are exactly the $T$-invariant subspaces. Thus module language links ring theory to representation theory.
intuition: A submodule is a region closed under every allowed scalar action. Quotienting turns each parallel additive coset into one new point, and invariance ensures the action descends.
pitfall: A subspace need not be invariant. Under the full matrix ring acting on $F^n$, the only submodules are zero and the whole space; a single chosen operator can have many.
prompt: Set the off-diagonal entry to zero and compare the two coordinate axes. Then introduce a shear term. Which axis stays invariant, and what does the quotient remember?
proof: If $v^{\prime}=v+w$ with $w\in W$, then $rv^{\prime}-rv=rw\in W$. Hence the quotient action is independent of representatives. Inverse image under the quotient map identifies submodules of $M/W$ with submodules of $M$ containing $W$.

worked.title: Quotient a cyclic module

title: Generation does not guarantee a basis
intuition: Module generators need not be independent. Quotients can introduce relations among them.
explanation: A module is finitely generated if a finite list spans it under scalar multiplication and addition. It is cyclic if one generator suffices and free if it has a basis giving unique coefficients. A short exact sequence says that $i$ is injective, $q$ is surjective and $\operatorname{im}i=\ker q$. It splits if there is a module map $s:Q\to M$ with $qs=\operatorname{id}$; then $M$ is a direct sum of the image of $i$ and the image of $s$.
proof: For each $m$, write $m=(m-sq(m))+sq(m)$. The first term lies in $\ker q=\operatorname{im}i$, and the second lies in $\operatorname{im}s$. If $s(x)$ also lies in $\ker q$, then $x=qs(x)=0$, so the intersection is zero. Both summands are submodules because all maps are module maps.
pitfall: The cyclic module $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ is not free over $\mathbb Z$: its nonzero generator satisfies the relation $2m=0$. Finite generation is not the same as finite length or freeness.
prompt: For relation 6e=0, predict the kernel of the quotient map from Z.
objective: Distinguish generators from bases and split from nonsplit exact sequences.

worked.title: A quotient of C₄ does not split
steps: The reduction map $\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ has kernel $\{0,2\}$, itself a copy of $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$.
A section must send $[1]$ to an odd residue, either one or three. But twice either candidate equals two modulo four, not zero.
Thus no additive section exists. The middle module is not $C_2\oplus C_2$, although both have four elements. Exactness does not imply splitting.

practice.question: Why is $\mathbb Q$ not finitely generated as a $\mathbb Z$-module?
practice.hint: Take a common denominator for a hypothetical finite list.
practice.answer: If all generators have denominators dividing $d$, every integer combination lies in $(1/d)\mathbb Z$. The rational number $1/(2d)$ does not lie there. Thus no finite list generates all of $\mathbb Q$.

explanation: For a commutative ring, the annihilator is an ideal, and the action factors through the quotient by it. For example integers modulo $n$, viewed as a module over the integers, have annihilator $n$ times the integers.
intuition: A module homomorphism commutes with every scalar action. The annihilator records which scalars act as zero on the entire module.

title: GL and SL: what must a transformation preserve?

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

intuition: A matrix is a rule for moving an entire coordinate frame. Invertibility means the frame never collapses; determinant one means its oriented volume is unchanged.
explanation: Here $n$ is a positive integer and $F$ is a field. Over the real numbers, the absolute determinant gives volume scaling and its sign gives orientation. The determinant homomorphism forgets the details of the deformation and remembers one scalar. Special orthogonal matrices preserve both inner products and orientation, a stronger condition than determinant one: a shear can belong to SL without preserving lengths.
proof: The determinant is multiplicative and is onto because diag(a,1,…,1) has determinant a for every nonzero a. Apply the first isomorphism theorem. Over a field of $q$ elements, choose the columns successively: the next column must avoid the span of the previously chosen columns, which contains $q^j$ vectors after $j$ independent choices.
pitfall: Determinant one does not imply orthogonal. Volume language applies to real matrices; the finite-field count uses linear independence rather than Euclidean volume.
prompt: Trace the determinant map and its kernel in the diagram. Compare the conditions defining GL, SL and O in the matrix lab.

worked.title: Determinant one does not imply orthogonality
steps: The shear $T=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant one, so it lies in $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb R)$. Its columns are not perpendicular, so it is not orthogonal.

The determinant map onto $F^\times$ is surjective: $\operatorname{diag}(a,1,\ldots,1)$ has determinant $a$ for every nonzero $a$. Its kernel is $\operatorname{SL}_n(F)$, giving the quotient by the first isomorphism theorem.

practice.question: Which condition fails for $\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$?

practice.answer: The determinant is zero, so it is not invertible and is not in GL. It is a valid linear map, but cannot represent an invertible group action.

title: Flags: a line inside a plane

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory
source.section: §5 Parabolic Subgroups: complete flags and flag stabilizers

intuition: A flag remembers a sequence of nested directions. In three dimensions, preserve a line and then the plane containing it; this forces a triangular pattern in the matrix.
explanation: We use column vectors and left actions throughout. Preserving the first line forces the first column to have only its first entry nonzero. Preserving the first plane forces the third entry of the second column to vanish. Invertibility then makes every diagonal entry nonzero. A partial flag omits some intermediate dimensions; its stabilizer is a parabolic subgroup.
theorem: B=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}a&b&c\\0&d&e\\0&0&f\end{pmatrix}:adf\ne0\right\},\qquad \mathrm{GL}_3(F)/B\cong\{\text{complete flags in }F^3\}\quad\text{as sets with an action}.
proof: The column conditions are exactly preservation of each subspace in the standard flag. Every complete flag admits an adapted basis; the matrix with this basis as columns sends the standard flag to it, so the action is transitive. The map $gB \mapsto  g\cdot F_{0}$ is a well-defined equivariant bijection by the stabilizer criterion.
pitfall: This coset space is a set with a GL action, not generally a quotient group: $B$ need not be normal. For row/right conventions the triangular pattern must be translated consistently.
prompt: Follow the nested subspaces and ask which entries of a column-action matrix must vanish at each stage.
subject: Groups & symmetry

reading.title: Borel, parabolic and Levi structure
paragraphs: For a standard complete flag, its stabilizer is $B=U\rtimes T$, with $U$ upper unitriangular and $T$ invertible diagonal. A partial flag has a block upper triangular stabilizer $P=U_P\rtimes L_P$; its Levi factor is block diagonal and its unipotent radical has identity diagonal blocks.

The only subspaces invariant under the entire standard Borel are the initial coordinate subspaces. The parabolic subgroups containing that Borel are the corresponding staircase groups. The normalizer identity $P=N_G(U_P)$ recovers the parabolic from its unipotent radical.

Kolchin’s theorem says a subgroup consisting entirely of unipotent matrices has a common invariant complete flag, hence is conjugate into the upper unitriangular group. Its key step is a common fixed nonzero vector; quotient by that line and induct. This is stronger than triangularising each element separately.

title: Schur: maps between irreducible worlds

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

intuition: An equivariant map cannot carve a nontrivial invariant piece out of an irreducible representation. It either loses everything or identifies the whole representation with another.
explanation: Let $V$ and $W$ be nonzero irreducible modules. The kernel and image of an equivariant map are invariant subspaces. Irreducibility therefore leaves only two possibilities for each. Over the complex numbers, finite dimension gives the stronger scalar-endomorphism statement, since an endomorphism has an eigenvalue.
theorem: T\ne0\Longrightarrow T:V\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}W,\qquad \operatorname{End}_G(V)=\mathbb C I_V\quad(V\text{ irreducible, finite-dimensional over }\mathbb C).
proof: If $T$ is nonzero then its kernel cannot be all of $V$ and its image cannot be zero; irreducibility gives ker $T=0$ and im $T=W$. For a complex equivariant endomorphism choose an eigenvalue $\lambda$. The map $T-\lambda I$ is equivariant and has a nonzero kernel; the first statement forces $T-\lambda I=0$.
pitfall: The scalar conclusion need not hold over the real numbers. Nonzero vector spaces are required in the definition of irreducibility.
prompt: Compare a nonzero map between irreducible modules with a projection from a reducible module. Which invariant kernel is permitted?
subject: Modules & representations
objective: Distinguish the two statements of Schur’s lemma.

worked.title: Endomorphisms over different fields
steps: If an intertwiner between irreducible modules is nonzero, its kernel and image are invariant. The kernel must be zero and the image the whole target; thus it is an isomorphism.
For a finite-dimensional irreducible complex module, an endomorphism $T$ has an eigenvalue $\lambda$. The map $T-\lambda I$ has a nonzero kernel, so Schur forces it to be zero.

Over $\mathbb R$, the quarter-turn matrix commutes with every plane rotation. It is a nonscalar endomorphism of the real irreducible $C_3$ plane module, so the scalar conclusion requires its field hypothesis.

practice.question: Can a nonzero map between two nonisomorphic irreducible complex representations be an intertwiner?
practice.hint: Apply the kernel-image argument.
practice.answer: No. A nonzero intertwiner would be an isomorphism, contradicting the assumption. The zero map is always an intertwiner.

title: Orthogonality turns traces into multiplicities

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory
source.section: §15 The Character Table: row orthogonality; S₃ example

intuition: Irreducible characters act like perpendicular measuring directions. Weight each conjugacy class by its size, take an inner product, and the result tells you how many copies of an irreducible representation are present.
explanation: Let $G$ be finite and all representations finite-dimensional over the complex numbers; $\chi ^{i}$ are its irreducible characters. For $S_{3}$ the conjugacy classes have sizes 1, 3 and 2, represented by the identity, a transposition and a three-cycle. In this order the irreducible characters are (1,1,1), ($1,-1,1$) and ($2,0,-1$). Their dimensions satisfy $1^{2}+1^{2}+2^{2}=6$. The square of the standard character is (4,0,1), so the tensor square contains one copy of each irreducible.
proof: Proof idea for orthogonality: average the group action on Hom(V,W) to project onto equivariant maps. Its trace is the character inner product. Schur’s lemma makes this dimension 1 for equal irreducibles and 0 for distinct ones. Additivity gives the multiplicity formula. For the displayed tensor square, all three weighted inner products are 1, and the dimensions sum to 4.
pitfall: Do not take an unweighted dot product of table rows. Complex conjugation is part of the inner product, even when every entry in this particular table is real.
prompt: Select two $S_{3}$ irreducibles to tensor. Check every multiplicity with weights 1, 3, 2 and verify the total dimension.
subject: Modules & representations

reading.title: Orthogonality and reading normal structure
paragraphs: The irreducible rows are orthonormal for $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle=|G|^{-1}\sum_C|C|\alpha(C)\overline{\beta(C)}$. Column orthogonality gives $\sum_i\chi_i(g)\overline{\chi_i(h)}=0$ for nonconjugate elements and $|C_G(g)|$ for equal classes. A character decomposes with nonnegative integer coefficients obtained from row inner products.

Twisting an irreducible by a linear character preserves irreducibility. Virtual characters allow integer coefficients, and norm one means an irreducible character or its negative. For an actual character, norms one, two and three force a sum of that many distinct irreducibles; the restriction on the norm matters.

The kernel of a character consists of classes where $\chi(g)=\chi(1)$. Every normal subgroup is an intersection of irreducible kernels. Inflation gives a bijection between irreducible complex characters of $G/N$ and irreducible complex characters of $G$ whose representation kernels contain $N$: compose the quotient representation with $G\to G/N$. Conversely, a representation trivial on $N$ descends uniquely to $G/N$; its invariant subspaces are unchanged. Twice the trivial character is a character but is not irreducible. The scalar sets $Z_\chi=\{g:|\chi(g)|=\chi(1)\}$ recover the center by intersection, and successive quotient tables detect nilpotence. The normal-subgroup data also determines solvability.

source.title: Alperin & Bell · Groups and Representations

reading.title: Nine character-table constructions
paragraphs: For $C_n$, all irreducibles are $\chi_j(g^k)=e^{2\pi ijk/n}$. For a direct product, multiply one irreducible character from each factor. Thus every finite abelian group has only linear irreducibles. A permutation character counts fixed points; its inner product with the trivial character counts orbits. Linear characters factor through the abelianization.

For $S_3$, class sizes $1,3,2$ yield rows $(1,1,1)$, $(1,-1,1)$ and $(2,0,-1)$. For $S_4$, use its quotient $S_3$, the permutation module minus the trivial line, and the sign twist; the degrees are $1,1,2,3,3$.

The two nonabelian groups of order eight have the same ordinary character table: four linear rows and a degree-two row $(2,-2,0,0,0)$ with the central classes first. The table alone therefore does not identify the group. For $A_5$, orthogonality gives degrees $1,3,3,4,5$ and the golden-ratio entries on the two five-cycle classes.

source.title: Alperin & Bell · Groups and Representations

reading.title: Practice routes: dihedral, symmetric and quotient tables
paragraphs: For the dihedral group of order $2n$, the degree-two rows have rotation values $2\cos(2\pi jk/n)$ and zero reflection values. Separate the even and odd cases: the number of linear characters changes because the abelianization changes.

To build the table of $S_5$, organize columns by cycle partitions, start with trivial and sign, use the degree-four standard representation and its sign twist, then construct exterior and symmetric squares and subtract known constituents. The final degrees are $1,1,4,4,5,5,6$, whose squares sum to $120$.

For quotient exercises, first identify which rows contain the chosen normal subgroup in their kernel, then merge the appropriate quotient classes. Check dimensions, weighted row norms and column centralizer sizes after every construction.
